speechtext:
May I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister encourage and the government assist in arranging a broad international conference of scientists to discuss the dangers of thermonuclear war, as proposed in a letter signed by six of the Soviet union's outstanding scientists and quoted in the leading editorial of the New York Herald Tribune of November 8?
Is he aware that the proposal has been endorsed by the editor of the bulletin of the atomic scientists and approved by Mr. Cyrus Eaton, who arranged the Pugwash scientific conference last summer?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: PROPOSED INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE OF REPRESENTATIVES OF SCIENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to do me the courtesy of sending me notice of his question, together with the editorial in the New York Herald Tribune, and also the observation thereon by Mr. Cyrus Eaton.
From a perusal of the editorial I conclude that the proposal made by the scientists of the U.S.S.R. was one outside of governmental consideration. Apparently a number of U.S.S.R. scientists suggested that it would be helpful if the atomic scientists of all countries and representatives of other disciplines, biologists, medical scientists, philosophers, economists, historians, sociologists and educators, could meet to express their weighty opinions in a broad international meeting of the most important representatives of science. Later on in the course of the letter these words appear:
The danger which hangs over mankind because of the possibility of using atomic energy for war purposes is common to all countries independent of their political and economic systems.
There is nothing in any way to prevent such a meeting under the auspices of any of the nations in respect of which representation by scientists would take place.
The basis of the meeting would be similar to the meeting convened in Pugwash, Nova Scotia, by Mr. Cyrus Eaton, at which representatives of various nations met and discussed international and scientific problems. This is not a conference for governments. It is one for scientists, and I would simply say that everything that can be done should be done to bring about peace in the world. If the scientists choose to meet I am sure there would certainly be every approval by the free nations. Further than that I cannot go at this time, for it is not a matter of national government consideration.

maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: PROPOSED INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE OF REPRESENTATIVES OF SCIENCE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. The point of my question was, will the government encourage and assist as far as its ability goes? I notice that Mr. Cyrus Eaton, in the article to which I referred and which I sent the Prime Minister, suggests that encouragement might be given by Canada and the conference might be held in Canada. The point of my question is, will the government encourage and to the extent that is possible assist in the organization of such a conference? I think we have scientists in Canada connected with the Chalk River project and the national research council who might be encouraged to join in organizing such a conference.

maintopic: ATOMIC ENERGY
subtopic: PROPOSED INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE OF REPRESENTATIVES OF SCIENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, up to the present time there has been nothing official in this connection except for a reference in the press to a suggestion made by certain scientists of the U.S.S.R. I would not want to go further at this time until an invitation was actually received by Canadian scientists. I notice that Mr. Cyrus Eaton says that such a conference would probably be held in Canada, the West Indies or India. Then he goes on to say that perhaps Canada might be the place of meeting. Certainly there was no interference in any way by the government of Canada with Soviet scientists coming to Canada to the conference convened by Mr. Eaton, and subject to any eventualities in the meantime I am sure the same attitude should be exhibited by the government in reference to any bona fide effort being made by scientists to discuss the problems of today and arrive at some solution which would ensure coexistence and peace in the world.

The Address-Mr. Pickersgill SPEECH FROM THE THRONE

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, November 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. A. R. Smith (Calgary South) for an address to Her Majesty the Queen in reply to her speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin what I have to say today by extending very sincere congratulations to the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) upon the excellent form of the speech he delivered in the house last evening. I think there is no doubt that the hon. member caught the ear of the house, which I assume is one of the first objects of a good new member, and I hope that as time goes on the hon. member will continue to bring forward in this house the problems of the province of Newfoundland, about his concern for which I express no doubt; and I am sure he expresses no doubt about mine.
I am afraid, however, that I cannot congratulate the hon. member upon having caught the ear of the Prime Minister, because when the hon. member used that nasty word "unemployment", which no Tory backbencher is supposed to use, there was a frown on the face of the Prime Minister, and I could only conclude that the party whip had not got all the way around with the warning that this nasty word "unemployment", which the Liberals use to spread doom and gloom in the country, was not to be used by Tory backbenchers. But no doubt the hon. member will learn in time.
Now, sir, I think the hon. member for St. John's East in his zeal did rather exaggerate the situation in the province of Newfoundland. It is true that there is a good deal ot unemployment there-more than twice as much as there was a year ago-and it is true that unless some steps are taken to improve that situation there will be a good deal more before the winter is out. That is a matter of proper concern to every member of this house, whatever province he happens to represent.
I suggest it would be better if the government, instead of suggesting that we should ignore the existence of unemployment, were to get busy and try to do some things which could be done, and done right away, to alleviate the unemployment situation. I do not think the hon. member for St. John's East will question my statement when I say that were it not for the building of two public buildings by the public works department and the building of a terminal at Torbay by the Department of Transport, projects undertaken

The Address-Mr. Pickersgill by the previous government, there would be a good deal more unemployment at St. John's than there is at the present time.
I must say that I feel a little concerned on reading stories in the press recently that other public works are going to be cut out for reasons of economy. We all know that the former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, in preparing his estimates-in fact he told the house this-did cut down the public works projects that were put into the estimates for this year, because at that time the prospect for private construction in this country was very good.
Now, for some reason or other

and I am not going to suggest what the reason is- those prospects are not nearly as good today, and I do think it is very unwise on the part of the government to be cutting out any of those essential projects at this particular time when all of us have a proper concern about a tendency toward increased unemployment, which I do not intend to exaggerate.
I should also extend the customary congratulations to the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault). I think they both did very well, but I do not think anything I can say would add to the congratulations that others have extended to them. I will, however, Mr. Speaker, extend a special word of congratulations to you. Like my hon. friend from Inverness-Richmond, I can say this with the more assurance because it is rather long delayed. I confess, sir, that when the names of the ministers were announced on June 21 many of us were astonished that your name was not among them. It did seem to us that you had made a great mark in this house and in other places, and it did seem astounding that you should not have been in the ministry; but the loss to the government, I think, sir, has been a gain to parliament. I believe you have already demonstrated that your main concern is to be utterly impartial and, speaking for myself, I would never ask anything more of the Speaker.
I want to express my admiration of the Prime Minister's election campaign. I think it is well known to the house that I have had a reasonably close association with other prime ministers of this country for what is now 20 years, and I must say that when I looked at the schedule of the Prime Minister's election engagements I was horrified. I thought the hon. gentleman or his advisers had mistaken him for superman. I must say that I never expected him to get to the end of the course. For sheer endurance I think it was a terrific record, for which I cannot fail to express my admiration.
[Mr. Pickersgill.)
I would also like, sir, to express to the Prime Minister my own appreciation of the way in which he has preserved the amenities of his office outside the house. I think he has done that admirably and we have all appreciated it. In doing so I think he was following the example set by my right hon. leader and I would suggest, sir, that if the Prime Minister would follow that example in the house as well as outside, the whole tone and temper of the house might be even better.	.
I should also like to say that I personally feel the Prime Minister should be congratulated upon the excellent arrangements that were made for, and carried out during, the royal visit. I do not think they could have been improved upon. I certainly personally have no criticism, and I do not think anyone in this party has any criticism, of the Prime Minister for having delayed the opening of the house in order to have it opened by Her Majesty. As a matter of fact, sir, I think it would be very ill-becoming any member of the Liberal party to express any such criticism, because in delaying the opening the Prime Minister was simply carrying out, and carrying out admirably, the plans which were already made by the previous prime minister.
I would also like to say, sir, that it was a source of particular gratification to me personally that the Prime Minister went to Washington as the minister in attendance upon the Queen. It did seem to me that was the right and proper thing to do; but my mind, sir, went back 18 years, to the first time a Canadian prime minister attended in Washington and in the United States as the principal adviser to the Canadian sovereign-a prime minister also from Prince Albert-and I could not fail to remember, sir, that at that time there were many members of the Conservative party who were very critical of what Mr. Mackenzie King did. But it is interesting to see that after a generation's lag the Tories usually decide that what Liberals have done is right.

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Since the large percentage of those residing in the Battle River-Camrose federal riding which it is my privilege to represent are either directly or indirectly dependent upon agriculture for their livelihood, it is my intention this morning to spend some time discussing a few of the problems that face those who are engaged in the major industry to be found in Canada. There is no need of my pointing out to the house that those engaged in this industry now find themselves in a position where, while they represent 17 per cent of our national population, their share of the national income was slightly above 6.9 per cent. This points out that those engaged in agriculture from coast to coast, and not in any one regional area alone, have been unfairly treated throughout the last number of years.
The agricultural policy of the Social Credit group has been well known not only to the members of this house but to the people of

The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith Canada for many years. It has not been a policy that has been adjusted in order to satisfy the changing winds of public opinion. It is not a policy that was drafted to satisfy regional groups in Canada. It is a truly national policy, an agricultural policy for all those engaged in that industry. We as a group are extremely proud of the agricultural policy we have advocated down through the years in this house. It is for this reason that it is my intention this morning to again put this policy on record.
In order that the farmers of Canada may be afforded the opportunity to obtain a fair share of Canada's national income, we of the Social Credit group advocate the following agricultural program. First, low cost and long-term credits to farmers and cash advances against the grain stored on the farms. Second, we advocate a two price system for the sale of our farm products. Products would be sold at parity prices on the domestic market and those exported abroad would be sold at the best price obtainable, preferably under international agreement, but supported at levels which would assure that the aggregate sales in the domestic and export market would return to the farmer his fair share of the national income. Third, we advocate the continuation of the Canadian wheat board as the sole marketing agency for wheat, oats and barley, with the inclusion of flax and rye to be handled under the jurisdiction of that board.
Fourth, we advocate an expansion of permanent storage for grain so the desired reserves of grain might be carried without interfering with the normal handling of the current crop. Fifth, an all-risk national crop insurance act along lines similar to the act now in operation in the United States of America. Sixth, the expansion of markets for farm products, (a) in the domestic market by equating the effective purchasing power with the aggregate of all prices of goods available for sale, and (b) externally by making surplus products available to all nations which are unable to obtain them through the normal channels of trade, by the acceptance of foreign currency, by barter deals and in the case of extreme distress by outright gifts.
We believe such a program is not merely in the interests of the Canadian farmer but that it is of vital concern to the people of Canada, in order to ensure that there will continue to be adequate supplies of food at fair prices, prices that bear a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities. Moreover, we feel it is of vital concern in helping to promote world peace.

I wish to point out that we of this group are not prepared to admit that there is a surplus of food in the world today, and in this opinion we have the backing of outstanding leaders in Canada at this time. I have in my hand a short article taken from the Wheat Pool Budget of August 16, 1957. This article deals with surplus disposal as follows:
To those who think that in agriculture we have arrived at a point where we need no longer expand I say to you this:	I learned one lesson at the
commonwealth conference in London-we must expand our agricultural development. With one quarter of the world's population going to bed hungry at night methods must be found to enable-
I want to stress this.
-to enable the distribution of our surpluses to the end that happiness will come to the peoples of the world.
These are not the comments of a wheat pool delegate from western Canada, nor of an official of the farmers' union in Alberta or the interprovincial farm union council. These are the words of the Prime Minister of Canada spoken to 11,000 people at the opening of the Saskatoon exhibition on July 22. We feel very definitely that the only reason we have a grain surplus in Canada today is because of faulty marketing and financial policies followed by the previous administration. No nation in the world should ever be plagued with surpluses of food when there are millions of hungry people in other areas.
We will admit that it is perhaps a wise policy to maintain in Canada a surplus of wheat and other foodstuffs at all times as a safeguard against possible crop failures and so forth, but we do not feel it is fair to expect the farmers of Canada to finance any great portion of such a surplus. It is a problem of national concern and should be financed by the nation as a whole.
The previous administration frowned upon such suggestions as the establishment of permanent storage facilities for our wheat and other grain. That same administration frowned upon the acceptance of sterling or the currency of other lands in return for agricultural products. It frowned upon barter deals and it frowned upon outright gifts of surpluses of food products to hungry nations. I sincerely hope that Her Majesty's present government will take a new look at this whole situation and attempt to place the food we have in surplus in Canada today into the mouths of those people who are hungry in other parts of the world.
During the last two sessions of parliament we in this house have spent considerable time discussing amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. During those discussions we of this group urged that several changes be made in

this act. We suggested that the maximum loan granted be increased from $15,000 to $20,000; that the time of repayment of a loan be extended from 30 to 40 years; that the amount of the loan which is granted upon the appraised valuation be extended from 65 to 80 per cent. We urged that there be a reduction in the interest rates charged on such loans, and finally we asked that a more realistic approach be taken to the whole matter of appraising farm property in order to bring such appraisals in line with the present day values of such properties.
We still feel that the act as it now stands is of little or no use to a young man who wishes to enter the agricultural industry. During last summer I had several farmers come to me with their complaints of being unable to secure assistance from the Canadian farm loan board. The interprovincial farm union council in their brief submitted to the Prime Minister and his cabinet on August 15 had this to say concerning the activities of the Canadian farm loan board:
There has been available for some considerable time the facilities of the Canadian farm loan board, but these have proven to be totally inadequate in performing the function, with respect to the farm finance, that we would anticipate from this board.
From experience, farmers (particularly young people wishing to establish themselves on farms) have found the operations of the Canadian farm loan board extremely restrictive.
In actual practice it would appear that the only people who have ready access to the facilities of this board are those who already have more land and greater assets than are normally required. In the words of the interprovincial farm union council, which represents farmers in the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario:
Our main concern in this respect is to enable young farmers to obtain the finances necessary, backed by the assets of the farm unit, to enable them to take over, in many cases, their fathers' farms and to allow them to carry on in the vocation for which they are best qualified.
Then again, on July 31 of last year the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet received a presentation from the Canadian federation of agriculture, and that presentation also dealt at some length with the Canadian farm loan board. It had this to say:
The regular Canadian farm loan board program also requires revision. Primarily-
And these are interesting words, Mr. Speaker.
-it needs to liberalize its present over-cautious and conservative appraisal and lending policies.

Mr. Speaker, in the industrial part of my riding are located, among others, the various elements which constitute the packing industry. Because of this proximity, and further because as a member of the Toronto board of health I have been keenly interested in this matter, I should like to bring to the attention of this house the problems arising out of the present, primitive and inhumane method used in the slaughter of our food animals.
It seems that in this field Canada has been lagging badly in taking the necessary legislative steps which other countries, no more progressive than we, long ago adopted. The broad principle of humane slaughter for our food animals may be enunciated as follows; that no animal being slaughtered for food purposes should be shackled, hoisted, hung, cut, bled or scalded without first having been rendered unconscious and insensible to pain in a humane manner.

In the case of ritual slaughter, Mr. Speaker, the present preparatory methods of shackling, hoisting and, so on, are deplorable. In England and in other countries the casting pen and other means have been used which eliminate the most inhumane aspects of ritual slaughter. Humane slaughter or slaughter practices by which animals are rendered unconscious and insensible to pain prior to being slaughtered is compulsory by legislation in many countries.
Under the Criminal Code of Canada it is an offence to cause unnecessary pain or suffering to an animal or bird. What in effect is being asked is that this broad statement be defined in such a way that the current primitive and inhumane methods will be discontinued. For the workers in packing house plants the present methods are laborious, unpleasant and unsafe, the accident rate in this connection being one of the worst of any industry on the continent.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that to the credit of some of the packing house operators in my riding they are adopting more up to date practices. However, until this government passes the necessary legislation, allowing the packers adequate time in which to carry out studies and plant changes, with an effective date, we shall not be able to march abreast of those other civilized countries which met this challenge many years ago.
At this time I should like to pay tribute to those kind people who have taken such great interest in this subject. Among those who have given outstanding service in this crusade I cannot help but mention Mr. George Bryant, who is a newspaper writer in Toronto. His countless articles on this subject have contributed much to public opinion.
I was happy indeed to hear that the meat packers' council of Canada has notified the government that "it welcomes the introduction of federal humane slaughter legislation". Along with the O.S.P.C.A., which has been spearheading this crusade for some time, and in conjunction with the packers, I believe that, if this government could now present to this parliament the necessary resolution which would embody the principles to which I have referred, then the bill could be presented later this session as soon as proper regulations could de drawn up. The important thing, however, Mr. Speaker, is that we in this house by our support of such a resolution could contribute immensely toward the almost immediate cessation of these primitive and inhumane methods used in the slaughter of our food animals.
I should now like to say a few words with regard to a problem which affects the

metropolitan Toronto area and the surrounding municipalities, all in all an area of about 1,000 square miles, which is represented in this house by 21 hon. members. As an executive member of the metropolitan Toronto and region conservation authority I am especially interested in the solution of this problem which affects about one-tenth of the people of Canada who live in this area.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, three years ago hurricane "Hazel" caused 80 deaths on one of the several rivers which drain this area. At that time the government of Canada contributed a considerable sum of money for flood relief in this region as well as men and equipment from military and civil services, for which indeed, the people of this area were most grateful. However, a scheme is now being prepared which would permanently solve this problem, provided federal aid were made available in conjunction with provincial assistance.
The cost of this permanent flood protection would be in the order of about $30 million, a sum far too great to be assumed by the real estate taxpayers in the area. I realize that there are similar problems in other parts of the country; and I would therefore urge the government to work out a detailed formula which could be applied to any such project so that local authorities might be able to prepare plans, having a definite goal in sight. The government should determine a cost-benefit ratio policy on such projects, based not only on primary and direct benefits but also on secondary benefits which would include both tangibles, such as resulting public parks, and intangibles such as the avoidance of epidemics, the facilitation of national defence and so forth.
As a firm believer in conservation I was very happy indeed to hear in the speech from the throne that at long last Canada will see the beginning of a national development policy which, carried out with the co-operation of the provinces and the territories, will enable all regions of Canada to share in the benefits to be realized in developing the resources of this great nation. There is no doubt in my mind that we stand on the threshold of a great and glorious era in the history of Canada, provided we are realistic with regard to this most important aspect of our economic development.
It was most gratifying to hear the Minister of National Defence announce the change in emphasis from militia training to civil defence organization. This is just another accomplishment of a government which has been in office for only a short time but having new and vigorous ideas. This government I am sure will not only produce efficiency in defence spending but
The Address-Mr. Kucherepa also, and this is most important, prepare our country properly for a challenge we hope our people will never have to face. Preparedness, Mr. Speaker, is an old motto but not an outmoded one. No matter how devastating an attack may be, indeed the more devastating it is,-the greater will be the need for a strong civil defence organization.
Civil defence is necessary to care for survivors, to organize essential services, provide for shelter, transportation and all those things necessary to keep body and soul together in trying times. Without civil defence there can be little hope of survival in the atomic era. In this age of expansion it is necessary that our soldiers be trained not only as effective combatants but also as efficient civil service personnel. Only through successful civil defence operations can we hope to reach the point where we will be able to carry out the final military operations necessary for a successful conclusion of any hostilities which might arise.
The best defence against possible disaster in the years which lie ahead, is a strong dependence on self-reliance, based on superior scientific knowledge but without the sacrifice of the humanities. This can only be attained by the further establishment and dramatic expansion of our educational and scientific institutions. We hope this nation can fully avail herself of her tremendous God given resources of brainpower which are being allowed to waste away because of the inability, for various reasons, of those responsible in this field of human endeavour to harness this latent potential of our people in the interests of peace and humanity. It was indeed gratifying to hear the assurances of the Prime Minister in this regard made in this house last week.
The world situation in many respects is alarming, but let us not lose faith. We in Canada, constituted as we are of many peoples from many lands, have a vital role to play which can do much to bring peace and stability to a troubled world. Discouraging as the situation may appear to some people, let me say that we in the free world, especially we in Canada, have an advantage which all the weapons, bombs, sputniks and muttniks cannot overcome. It is not only a moral advantage but a physical one, through the bonds of consanguinity which we have with the tens of millions of people who today are enslaved by that international tyrant called communism.
Their enslavement, which we hope will soon end through the efforts of free people everywhere, is a prevailing state of affairs which will in effect hold back any insidious

The Address-Mr. Kucherepa intentions the Russian leaders may have toward world expansion, until one day the core of communism, being what it is, will crack up and go the way of all dictatorships. When it does we, through our various efforts in the British commonwealth of nations, in NATO, through assistance to underdeveloped countries and especially by our efforts in the United Nations, will have made a real contribution, worthy of our heritage, in helping to bring freedom to nations now enslaved in one form or another by modern Russian imperialism, which at present disguises itself under the cloak of international communism.
To hear these communists rant and rave and disseminate falsehoods about Great Britain, which country has brought through education and evolution freedom, democracy and self government to many former colonies and formerly backward peoples, is a colossal violation of the truth which history will one day expose, even as it will reveal the insidious and brutal methods that communists have used to enslave one nation after another until today most of eastern and central Europe is under their domination.
Many of the people who are today subjected to communism are nations that only two score years ago won their freedom and independence after centuries of enslavement. I predict that they will be free again, for I believe that truth and justice must one day triumph; and I know our efforts toward this end will win for us the eternal friendship of all these nations, most of whom are related and joined by racial ties to many of our Canadian people.
Much has been said about national unity by some of the hon. members in this house in weeks gone by. I could not understand the reasoning behind some of the remarks of these members, unless they were a manifestation of a kind of parochial thinking which most Canadian people had believed no longer existed in our country. I think most hon. members have heard on countless occasions exalted speakers of the Liberal party announce and reiterate the achievements of national unity amongst the people of Canada, which they claimed were built on rugged foundations which would forever hold. Now that the Liberal party has suffered a defeat at the polls it seems that in the opinion of some of the hon. members of that party this means the end of national unity in our country. If anything, I would say those revealing and startling remarks made by some of the hon. members opposite merely serve to underline the fact that the Conservative party which now forms the government has, as those speaking the truth always will,

emerged as a great Canadian party which represents all the provinces and all the groups which constitute this great Canada of ours.
I want to say that our party by virtue of its composition, built as it is on this broad national foundation and having as it does representatives from not only the two great ethnic groups of which some hon. members have spoken but also from other important groups, ethnic and otherwise, will jealously guard the rights of all minorities, big or small, notwithstanding the fact that a particular group may, on occasion, and for quite plausible reasons, support more strongly some other party.
I do not think there is anything remarkable in this regard about the results of the June 10 election. Nine of our ten provinces contributed most of the increase in the number of seats held by the Conservative party in the House of Commons. The people of Canada wanted to change their government, and they voted for a Conservative administration. In so far as the people of Quebec are concerned they did what I consider to be rather a common thing in free elections; they supported what is known in political parlance as "their favourite son"; a man who is a great Canadian and who has always commanded a great deal of personal support in his home province, even as some other outstanding hon. members of this house, past and present, have commanded support in other years and in other parts of the country. That man of course is the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent).
I believe this is a common condition existing not only in Canada but in other democracies. What I do think is unfortunate for the members opposite is that right now, at least, there is not one among them who could possibly emulate that distinguished Canadian of whom I have just spoken. Therefore I have every confidence that when the opportunity presents itself the good people of the province of Quebec will join the people of the other nine provinces in supporting, in equal measure, the Conservative party which is today the living symbol of national unity in every sense of the word.
We have on this side of the house men and women who can trace their origin to almost every major ethnic group in Canada, including some very fine representatives, if I may say so, from the great province of Quebec, of whom we are justly proud and of whom we expect many more in the next parliament.
In conclusion I appeal to all hon. members of this house not only to preach national unity but to practice it inside and outside

these walls; for I firmly believe, as do most Canadians, that although there is not uniformity in all things amongst us, there is full agreement among Canadians in all those things which unite us.

In the
interests of saving the time of the house, Mr. Speaker, I will not extend congratulations to all those who have so richly deserved them since this debate began, but will content myself by associating myself in this regard with my leader, who so ably handed out the plaudits when he made his most excellent address.
Likewise I do not intend to spend any considerable time on the contents of the speech from the throne, chiefly because we have already dealt with a good part of it in the form of legislation, and the amendment now before the house very clearly states our position in that regard. We have indicated in our amendment approval of all those progressive measures which have been put before the house or which are still to come and to which we will give support because as a matter of fact they are part and parcel of what we have been advocating for some years.
At the same time our amendment sets before the house something rather more solid about which to think, and that is the question of dealing with the basic economic issues. Unless these are faced and solved, it will not be possible to hand out what might be called Christmas gifts in the next speech from the throne. We have to build a firm and solid economic base which will make it possible to produce the wealth, and so distribute that wealth as to bring about the best possible social security in this country.
There are two omissions in the speech from the throne to which I wish to refer, and I will do so briefly. One is the lack of any action with regard to federal aid to education. This is a question which has been raised in this house on numerous occasions. If I remember correctly, I was the one who first introduced the matter in the form of a resolution back in 1946, and the subject has been introduced and debated on nine or ten occasions since that time. The present Prime Minister, as I recall, together with a number of his colleagues, gave approval while in opposition to the proposition I put forward, but unfortunately I failed to find any reference to the matter in the speech from the throne, or any indication that the government is planning to do anything with regard to it at the present session of parliament. I hope they will come up with something before next session.
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
The other omission I wish to mention has already been referred to; that is the lack of any increase to war veterans under the Canadian Pension Act. It seems to me somewhat unfortunate that at a time when we have provided for a general increase all down the line under our social security measures, modest as it may be, we should not have seen fit to increase at the same time and a least in the same proportion the pensions which the Canadian veterans have so well earned.
The subject with which I wish to deal almost exclusively this afternoon is one which I consider to be a very important issue in this country at the present time, and which I predict may become one of the most important issues of all in the near future. I refer to the recent proposal made by the government of Great Britain to Canada to establish a free trade area between the two countries. In my opinion that offer was a historic event which unfortunately has been kept in the background so far as the present government is concerned. It is a very important issue for many reasons, but even if you look at the matter purely from the point of view of dollars and cents it is evident that it is time parliament faced this problem and dealt with it effectively at this present session, because it is obvious that the question of trade, tariffs and trade restrictions affects every Canadian at all times.
The house may be interested to know that in the last 10 years alone the Canadian people have paid out in the form of tariff duties for the goods they have imported from various countries overseas and to the south almost $4 billion. I have all the figures here before me. Obviously I cannot quote them all, but if we look up the records back to the time of confederation we will find we have paid out in customs duties and tariffs in this country more than Canada's total national debt.
This sum represents what has actually been collected in the form of revenue from the various duties. In addition the Canadian consumers have, in my opinion, paid a sum equal to if not greater than that amount in the form of prices which have been artificially inflated by those industries which have been able to increase their prices unduly because of the umbrella protection which our tariff structure provides for them. So if one takes into account what has been paid in actual cash into the public treasury in the form of tariffs, and adds the artificially high prices charged by industries which have produced goods protected by tariff barriers, we reach a fantastically high figure; and for that reason alone every Canadian should be interested in this particular question.
1010	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
I wish to place my stand on this question fairly and squarely before the house, if for no other reason than to provoke a real debate on the whole subject of a free trade area. So far as I recall it, only oblique references have been made to the matter in various parts of the house but no one has really dealt with it thoroughly. I wish to make a case to the best of my ability for the establishment of a free trade area between the United Kingdom and Canada. In my opinion Canada should accept the proposal made by the United Kingdom, and do so with great alacrity. There are strong and compelling reasons why we should do so, and I should like to place before the house five advantages which are to the obvious benefit of Canada, though this number does not by any means exhaust the list.
First, it would reduce the cost of living in Canada, a problem which is our No. 1 headache at the present time. Second, it would improve our export position with regard to primary products so far as the United Kingdom is concerned. Third, it would improve the quality of our consumer goods in Canada. Fourth, it would help to level out our trade balance; and fifth, it would be a step toward the solidarity of our commonwealth.
Now I wish to say a few words about each of these advantages. First a reference to the cost of living. This is a very important issue in Canada and it is one which is often, and in my opinion quite erroneously, referred to as inflation. I do not consider that the present unusually high cost of living in this country is a matter of inflation. Inflation, in the true sense of the word, is a condition in which there is a shortage of goods and services in relation to the availability of purchasing power. I am sure we will all agree that this is not the situation which exists in Canada at the present time; in fact, in regard to primary products the very opposite is the case. We are in a surplus position so far as agricultural products are concerned; we are in something of a surplus position so far as wood products are concerned; we are in a surplus position so far as base metals are concerned, and we seem to be quickly reaching a surplus position in the case of almost every primary product in this country.
So there is not a shortage of actual goods; that is not what is causing the condition which we call inflation, or the high cost of living. What is, in my opinion, causing the high cost of living is the systematic and arbitrary increase in prices on the part of those industries which enjoy either monopoly positions or near monopoly positions, and


which so operate that they take full advantage of the umbrella of protection which they have enjoyed for a long period of years.
In such a situation as this the establishment of an area of free trade between the United Kingdom and Canada would immediately open an alternative source of supply to the Canadian consumer. This does not mean that British-made goods would replace Canadian-made goods, but it would mean that the Canadian consumer would have an alternative choice, and the existence of an alternative choice of a source of supply would automatically tend to bring the prices of Canadian made goods somewhere near their true value rather than the inflated value now shown on the price tags.
Second, with regard to the export of primary products, it has been said by a number of hon. members in this house and elsewhere that the United Kingdom has been scrambling around for several years in an effort to raise dollars with which to buy Canadian products. The export-import figures indicate what the situation is at the present time. Taking the first six months of 1957, from January to June, which are the latest figures I can find, we see that we have exported to the United States in that period goods to the value of $1,391 million; but we imported from the United States goods to the value of $2,139 million, giving them a favourable balance of trade of about $800 million in a period of six months. In the same period we exported to the United Kingdom goods to the value of $341 million and imported from the United Kingdom goods to the value of $260 million, leaving us a favourable trade balance of $81 million.
That indicates a trend that has been developing over the years, and it is a trend which is dangerous both to Canada and to the United Kingdom. We have been buying more and more from the United States and attempting to sell more to the United Kingdom than we have been buying from her. Inevitably the time is going to come when the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries are going to say to themselves, "If we cannot sell our goods in Canada and so earn dollars with which to buy her exports to us we are going to have to look elsewhere for that opportunity". Therefore it is not surprising that Great Britain is becoming increasingly interested in a free-trade area on the continent of Europe. I warn hon. members, and the government particularly, that unless we show some interest in the proposal which was made to Canada by Great Britain for a free-trade area, then Great Britain may decide that we are simply not interested in carrying on any large volume of trade with her and will

almost inevitably give her attention to the building up of a free-trade area on the continent of Europe, and that could be disastrous to the export of our agricultural products in the future.
I come now to the question of the quality of consumer goods in Canada. In my opinion there has been a steady and a sad deterioration in the quality of manufactured goods in Canada since the war. In my opinion at the present time the Canadian consumer is the victim of jerry-built junk, which is sold through high pressure advertising and through appearance, new styles and new models, rather than through quality. Unfortunately the emphasis seems to be on appearance and on selling rather than on building goods which will serve. Goods are made to sell and not to serve. It is perhaps most evident with regard to the consumer goods in lines such as textiles, automobiles, electrical appliances, furniture and things of that kind. With the exception of certain types of heavy machinery and some of the building materials, it is my opinion that the consumer goods offered to the Canadian public by Canadian and United States manufacturers are now at an all-time low.
It might be interesting to interject at this point that it is rather strange that so far as the agricultural producers are concerned, we have built up a rather elaborate system of government grading of goods which are produced by the farmers, particularly at the producer level, so the consumer may be protected when he is buying food products that have been government-inspected, government-stamped and approved to show that they are of the proper quality and wholesomeness. But how many of our manufactured articles are government-inspected or government-approved? When a man buys an automobile, a radio, a television set, a pair of shoes or anything of that kind, and pays very high prices these days, what guarantee has he that he is getting the quality for which he is paying?
The benefit of a free-trade area with Great Britain would, in my opinion, help to improve this situation. British-made goods, over a period of years, have built up a world-wide reputation for quality. I think the manufacturers of Great Britain have followed a very sensible long-range policy in realizing that in the long run it is the quality of the goods and satisfied customers that bring the business; it is not a question of being able to put on a high-pressure selling job and move a whole volume of goods in a short time; to make a big profit, get in, get rich and get out. They are in business to stay, and they try to give the customer satisfaction. I think
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny it could act as a very good example for Canadian and United States manufacturers if they could put some of their goods within reach of the Canadian people so we could test their quality against the shoddy junk that is being offered on the Canadian market today.
I come now to the balance of payments. I have already mentioned the export and import figures as between Canada and the United States and Canada and Great Britain, but there is also a large amount of money involved in the question of interest and dividend payments. Here again we find that in the year 1956, the latest figures for a whole year, on the interest and dividend account we received from the United States $75 million, in round figures, but we paid to the United States in the same year $533 million, giving us a deficit of $458 million. We received from the United Kingdom $20 million; we paid out to the United Kingdom $72 million, leaving a deficit balance of $52 million. If we take all other countries together we find that we received from them $140 million and paid out to them $530 million, leaving a deficit for Canada of $390 million. If we add all these deficits together, on interest and dividend account we find that in 1956 we were in a deficit position to the extent of $900 million, almost a billion dollars.
There are two ways in which we could help to level out this enormous deficit on interest and dividend account. One of the ways would be for Canadians to invest more money in Canada rather than depend to such a great extent, as we have in the past, upon investment from the United States. I think this is a field which has yet to be properly explored. I would recommend to the government that they give rather more attention to this question than has been given in the past. Time will not permit me to go into all the various ways in which this could be done. I would recommend that the government ask some of the experts to study the field and try to find ways and means by which they could open up to the Canadian public avenues of investment in Canadian industries and in the development of Canadian resources, and to that extent stop leaning upon United States capital to such a fantastic extent as we have been doing in recent years.
Then there is another way in which we could help to level out that situation, and that would be by accepting sterling in exchange for some of our exports. So long as sterling remains unconvertible the best way in which we could dispose, or make use, of that blocked sterling we would receive would
1012	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny be to invest it in the commonwealth countries. In my opinion there is a large field for that purpose. I think Canada is suffering to some extent from a sort of national inferiority complex so far as finances are concerned. We have become too used to the idea that we have not any capital. I think it is a myth which has lived much longer than it has any right to live. We have been in a debtor position for so many years that we seem to think that is where we have to stay.
Now that the shoe is getting on the other foot I think we have the responsibility within the commonwealth and in the world generally to begin now to use the resources and the capital that we have in this country, not only to develop our own industries but in assisting to develop the industries and resources in some of the commonwealth countries which have not been so fortunate as we have been in recent years. By doing these two things, first investing some of our own money in our own industries rather than using foreign capital and, second, by accepting sterling as part payment for our export goods, we can materially reduce our deficits on interest and dividend account, and eventually I feel we can arrive at a surplus position.
I come to the fifth advantage I mentioned with regard to a free trade area between the United Kingdom and Canada, and that is the question of solidifying the commonwealth. I know when I say that it might sound more like a sentimental argument than an economic one, and it is perhaps a phrase that sounds rather platitudinous because it has been mentioned so often before. This idea of solidifying the commonwealth, Mr. Speaker, is something I suggest in all seriousness. History shows us that if we want to maintain a solid and lasting political entity such as the commonwealth which, in my opinion, is the most wonderful association of free peoples which has ever existed, then we must lay an economic basis in order to make that political entity possible.
We cannot keep the commonwealth together on pure sentiment. We must be prepared to show that as a nation we are ready to play the game within the family of nations which we call the commonwealth. We must be prepared to set an example to our members of the commonwealth by establishing the most solid economic relations possible with the United Kingdom. We must remember that the commonwealth now is a much larger entity, both in area and population, than it was only a few years ago. We have now the Asiatic and African peoples who belong to
[Mr. Zaplitny .1

the commonwealth. They are countries relatively new in relation to history, and I am sure they are looking to us as one of the senior or older members of the commonwealth to show an example of economic co-operation.
We talk about the political and economic freedom in the -world. Here we have right within the commonwealth a grand opportunity to accept and put into effect both political and economic co-operation, and if we fail to accept the proposition of the United Kingdom for the step by step, gradual building up of a free trade area I am afraid we will not be fulfilling our responsibility as a senior member of the commonwealth to accept something which is economically sound and politically necessary. A challenge has been given to us, and I hope there will be the statesmanship on the government benches that can accept the challenge and utilize it in the best interests of this nation and of Great Britain.
I would also add to the five advantages I have mentioned three specific steps that I believe would have to be taken within Canada in relation to the whole question of a free trade area with the United Kingdom. First, if we are going to make an effective job of it I believe we should set up an export-import board. So far as the disposal of our surpluses is concerned, I believe we are going to have to give greater attention to bulk sales and may even have to give some consideration to barter deals. Therefore an export-import board established for the purpose of most efficiently and intelligently organizing our trade within the free trade area is a must. It is a necessity. It is not a question of choice. I believe we should lose no time in setting up a board of that nature, made up of qualified personnel who would be given the duty and responsibility of exploring the whole field of a free trade area and finding the best means by which we could move the largest volume of goods both ways in order to make such a plan fully effective.
Second, I believe that as a nation we should make the greatest possible use within such free trade area of our co-operative movement both in Canada and the United Kingdom. It so happens that in our own country the co-operative movement has developed more or less along producer lines, and so far as the prairie provinces at least are concerned we now have a highly developed and very efficient system of producer cooperatives which have the know-how, the machinery and experience in that phase of the co-operative movement.
We have not advanced quite as rapidly in the consumer co-operative field. On the

other hand in Great Britain, particularly in Scotland, the consumer co-operative movement has developed rapidly and very soundly and efficiently. I thing we can make use of both phases of the co-operative movement. I think they complement each other, and I believe that within a free trade area, with proper government encouragement and cooperation, the co-operative movements of Canada and the United Kingdom can be important instruments in efficiently organizing two-way trade. I will not have the time to go into detail on this matter, but I feel very strongly that we as a parliament and the government have too long ignored and neglected the economic values in the cooperative movement, and should be prepared to make greater use of that movement.
Third, I would recommend that we make every effort as a parliament to make greater use of port Churchill in Manitoba. Port Churchill is the nearest seaport to the greater part of the three prairie provinces. It could be built into a large metropolis if it were given some encouragement. One way in which it could be given encouragement would be to make the greatest possible use of that port as a trading centre or port of entry and export with the United Kingdom. As a matter of fact I would go so far as to advocate that port Churchill be made a free port of entry for British-made goods. That in itself would provide great encouragement for the building up of facilities and the greater use of that port, and eventually would pay large dividends in western Canada.
That is the case I make at the present time for the acceptance by Canada of the offer made by the United Kingdom to this country. But I wish to say that since the proposal was made it seems to me we have had a thoroughly disappointing response on the part of the government. I do not wish to repeat this too often, but we know that the present Prime Minister, in campaigning throughout the country, repeatedly stated that he would like to see an increase in the trade between the United Kingdom and Canada. He made a specific proposal that he would attempt to divert about 15 per cent of our trade with the United States to Great Britain. That gave the people of Canada reason to believe that if a new administration took office the new government would take some specific steps immediately to make some sort of proposal to the United Kingdom.
You can imagine the shock that many of us who are keenly interested in this matter felt when not only did the government not make any proposals to the United Kingdom, but when the United Kingdom made its proposal the Canadian government seemed
The Address-Mr. Harrison to react in a sort of horrified manner as if to say well now, look, fellows; surely you did not need to take us quite that seriously. We did not really mean what we said. We were just talking in terms of elections, and now all of a sudden you come and offer us free trade.
I believe the government of Canada should have given approval to the principle of that proposal immediately, and should have begun immediately to lay some plans for putting it into effect. What they have done so far has been thoroughly disappointing. I am not of an unduly suspicious nature, Mr. Speaker, but if I were I could quote extracts from such newspapers as the Leader-Post of Regina, the Star-Phoenix of Saskatoon and the Free Press of Winnipeg, and also the words of Premier Matheson of Prince Edward Island, all of which, since that offer was made, have expressed the belief that the government is not interested in expanding the area of trade with Great Britain, is not interested in a free trade area, and feels that somehow in some way it is going to get itself off the hook on this matter without having to answer to the electors.
I hope for its own good the government will not attempt to do that as far as western Canada and the maritimes are concerned. In fact I doubt if they will get away with it even in central Canada, but certainly they will not get away with it so far as the prairie provinces are concerned. They have made certain pledges. Their leader has stated that he would divert a certain amount of trade from the United States to Great Britain. Now that the offer has been thrown in his lap we are sitting back and watching to see what he is going to do with it. No amount of excuses, no amount of dodging about is going to get him out of this situation. He is firmly committed to enlarging the area of trade with Great Britain. We feel that Great Britain has made a statesmanlike offer, a sensational offer, which should have been immediately accepted by Canada. We are waiting to see this indecision and bumbling, in which the Minister of Finance is becoming an expert, come to an end and have the Prime Minister rise in his place and announce that Canada is accepting in principle the British proposal and is taking concrete steps to put it into effect.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is some little time since I made a speech in this house, in fact it is some little time since I made a speech. I am making this one as the result of a promise I gave during the last election campaign to the effect that I would make a speech, not during the campaign but afterwards. I am therefore

The Address-Mr. Harrison in some danger, if I can last out the next 30 minutes, of fulfilling the only promise I made to my electorate during the last campaign. In that respect I am in a little more satisfactory position than some of those to your right, Mr. Speaker, who still have their troubles ahead of them.
When I went home at the end of the last session I found that the people were quite familiar with the issues of the campaign; in fact they were sick and tired of issues and speeches. As a matter of fact the only issue in my particular riding so far as I was concerned Was whether or not my constituents endorsed the kind of representation I had given them in the past, and particularly whether or not they endorsed the fact that I spend about $5,000 per year of my salary in covering the tremendous area that is mine to represent. This expenditure results from the fact that about 90 per cent of the constituency has to be covered by airplane. I made no promises in this regard during this campaign, because I had made the promise some 13 years ago and have kept it since. My only difficulty would arise if some of those who opposed me at the time gave some concrete guarantees that they would do the same as I had done. Since this situation did not arise there was not too much point in discussing issues, so far as I was concerned.
There has always been a bit of the minstrel in me and this came to the surface during the campaign, because I conducted most of my campaign with an orchestra and did not discuss any of the issues whatever. I was panned pretty hard by some of the newspapers in some editorials for this, but of course they did not know the background and the fact that the issues were fairly well under control as far as that area was concerned. What I was interested in was getting around to see as many people as possible. The idea of taking part in an acrimonious debate appealed neither to myself nor my electors at that moment.
Having made these preliminary remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall now get on with the proposition of fulfilling my promise to my electors, namely that I would make a speech after the election. During the early part of this debate I was intrigued by a line or two in a speech made by my good friend the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton). He was talking about the improvements that had come about under the new government in a very short time, and he said:
Take a look at the headlines. What a change there is from the last ten years.
I took the hon. member at his word and looked at a few headlines. I did not find his

contention was borne out by the headlines at	which I looked but perhaps	we
looked at different headlines. These are examples of the headlines that I found that were not common during the previous ten years when we had a Liberal government and when our economy was at such a high level that it was next to that of the United States who lead the world. I have picked these examples at random, and I shall read the headlines only: "Cost of Living Reaches 123.4, All-Time High"; "Grain Glut on Great Lakes Very Serious"; "Faltering Prices May be Portent of '58 Business"; "Predict Record Expansion Era to end Next Year"; "Business Failures Rise 16 Per Cent in Eight Months"; "Alberta Oil Demand Lowest since 1955"; "Canadian Stock Markets drop in Frantic Selling"; "Canadian Stock Markets Suffer Severest Losses"; "Stocks Fall Again, Uranium Off Most"; "Place 31 Per Cent Fewer, Job Vacancies Off"; "Jobless List Rises Sixth Straight Week"; "Unemployment Rises for Seventh Week in Row"; "Jobless Rolls Rise Sooner than Usual"; "450,000 Jobless This Winter, Labour Warns Diefenbaker"; "Hudson Bay Net off 60 Per Cent as Metal Prices Dip"; "Shutdown of Mines in B.C. is Becoming Increasingly Serious"; "Oil and Gas Export Policies Non-Existent while Industry Position Gets Worse Daily". Those are some of the headlines I noted, and certainly those are not the kind of headlines we read during the last ten years.
I will admit that this government has been in office for a short time, so one cannot expect too much to show for their efforts, but at least they could have maintained the economy in the same position in which they found it when they took over. From the standpoint of the west, and I am a western member, we have to look back through the years to see what Tory governments have done for the west in the past. Starting at the beginning, one would naturally start with Sir John A. Macdonald who, in this part of the country, is always looked upon as a great statesman. Perhaps he was in this part of the country, but some of his actions out west throw some doubt upon that point. I want to speak initially about his actions with regard to land tenure in the west.
At that time the northern part of the west was settled by the Metis, whose only mode of transportation was the river and lake systems. Naturally, therefore, these people settled on narrow strips of land which ran back some distance from the edge of the water. Then Mr. Macdonald introduced the idea that there would be a reorganization of the land system and all the plots of land would be square. This system in effect dispossessed

those people of their homes and although representations were made for ten years in a row, in the same hard-headed fashion that one still observes in the Conservative party the system was rammed down the throats of the people in the west. Naturally there was some resistance which was treated in the traditional Tory fashion, when the government brought out troops to deal with these people. They wound up by hanging Louis Riel who, so far as most of the west is concerned, is still looked upon as a patriot because all he did was lead the people who wanted to fight for their homes.
Well, that was our first brush with a Conservative government. Then the next man who came along was supposed to do much better for the west because he came from the west. He was the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Naturally he would have the welfare of the west at heart because he came from the west. But under R. B. Bennett we in the west suffered under the same policies originated by Mr. Macdonald. We suffered from a tariff policy that provided an umbrella to eastern manufacturers to which westerners had to pay a tribute of 25 per cent or 30 per cent in the way of duty.
Mr. Bennett continued in the same way. He came into power saying that he was going to blast his way into the markets of the world by putting in higher tariffs, something which he did. When he first came in he also said he would bring on a British trade conference. He held out great prospects of that conference relieving us of our ills in this country. I refer to these matters in order to show the parallel between what was done at that time and what is being held out to the people now and to indicate that it is about the same thing. When he got through blasting his way into the markets of the world we were in extremely bad shape in this country. In fact, this country was in the worst condition it has ever been in. That was the promise and that was the performance.
Now we come to the present government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I was rather intrigued to note that during this last election campaign no mention was made of the Conservative party in the west. Maybe their past record is a good enough reason for that. All their election signs said out there was "Diefenbaker". If you had a 20-power microscope you might see "Progressive Conservative" at the bottom of the sign. If I had the record that these people have I think I might have used some name like Diefenbaker or somebody else. I certainly would not put the name of my party on it.
The Address-Mr. Harrison
In the last campaign-although I did not take part in the discussions at that time for reasons I mentioned at the outset-the question arose as to whether the new John Diefenbaker was going to be any different from any other Tory leader we have ever had. Immediately the suggestion was put forward by those supporters that he has out there, "Well, John is from the west and he will not let the west down". I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that he is not the first Lochinvar who has come out of the west as far as the Conservative party is concerned. We all remember Mr. Bennett. He was from farther west than the Prime Minister, and he did not do so well for the west.
We start out with this new government and they are going to have a commonwealth conference instead of a British trade conference which is something of the same order, and they tell us that it is going to cure all our ills. To go on from there, they are going to shake a stick at the United States and they have been doing so for the last nine years that I have been here, from the opposition side of the house, and they were going to go down and tell those people what they were going to do. They were going to blast their way into some markets of the world by telling the United States off. We have had some indication that that has not taken place.
What other indications are there that the Prime Minister is not much different than his predecessors? Once he gets in the strait-jacket of Tory policy he cannot do too much for the west. He is in the same position as R. B. Bennett. Maybe his heart is in the right place and I do not doubt that it is. But when you get that kind of policy saddled on you you are not going to do the things that the west particularly wish.
That brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the attempt to get greater trade with Great Britain. The Prime Minister went over to the prime ministers' conference with the avowed intention of increasing trade with Great Britain. This is something that is dear to the west. They like that idea. I think he went there also with the idea that maybe he could do something along that line; but when he made his suggestion that they might change 15 per cent of their trade from the United States to that country, even the British papers cast a great deal of doubt on the possibility of doing that. When you look at Britain's position you find that she has just so many Canadian dollars with which to do business. I think the Prime Minister went there with his tongue in his cheek

The Address-Mr. Harrison or in other words he knew that with impunity he could make a good fellow of himself in the west by saying that we should have more trade with Great Britain, knowing that Great Britain could not accept that proposal.
But they fooled him. He went there and they said, "We should have free trade". Here is something that is right down the alley as far as western Canada is concerned. For years we have been paying tribute to eastern manufacturers. From the point of view of building up the country, there may be something to that idea. But it is rather hard to tell the people in the west that that is the situation. They have been paying tribute to the eastern manufacturers and they think it is about time that some of those industries stood on their own feet. When somebody tells you that you cannot have free trade, that is not correct. It must be approached with some caution, it is true. We have had some free trade in some items.
The last Liberal government arranged with the United States a proposition whereby we could have free trade in farm implements. At that time the Canadian manufacturers said that would be their ruination. Large companies such as the Massey-Harris company were loud in condemnation of that proposition at that time. Yet it was the best thing that ever happened because it opened to them a large market in the United States.
Free trade with Britain naturally does not come into the same classification as free trade with the United States because you are not dealing with like levels of population. But it has some merit as far as you can let it go without doing too much damage to our industries in this country. So when this present government turned down the proposition of Great Britain that over a period of years we would approach towards the goal of free trade, as far as the people out west were concerned, the Prime Minister, who comes from the west, had sold them down the river.
I do not think there is anyone who can tell them anything different. If he had said that he would look into the proposition and over a period of years would try to slacken tariff barriers between Great Britain and ourselves, I think they would have gone along with that proposition. But no mention is made of that at all. The whole Conservative party is appalled at the idea of going into any free trade with anybody. It is definitely against Conservative policy. So our friend from Prince Albert, who of his own volition would like to go along with this idea and who for 15 years has talked as the champion

of the farmers from the west, at the first opportunity that any Canadian has ever had to bring in free trade and the opportunity for farmers in the west to buy in the same market as that in which they are obliged to sell-and he is the first Canadian who has had that opportunity-has turned it down.
At the time this proposal was made by Great Britain I noticed some articles in the paper by heads of manufacturing concerns who would likely be hit if free trade was gone into, one of them being the head of a wire company-I think it was the Greening wire company-who said his costs of operation were of the order of 240 against Great Britain's 90. I used to be in the mercantile business in the west some years ago and when I came to this house in 1949 or just prior to that time I was selling barbed wire which is sold to most farmers who raise cattle. I was selling that item at a little bit over $5 a roll. I was surprised to find out this summer that it is now $15 a roll. Why is it $15 a roll? Because Mr. Greening, who gave his figures himself, has been allowed, under a system of protection, to raise his price to $15. That is at the retail level. He will not get that because there will be the cost of distribution and so on to be taken into consideration.
