speechtext: It has risen from $5 to $15?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It has risen in that way.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is barbed wire the only thing that has risen in price?

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is not the only thing that has risen in price but it is one thing that has risen where this one man connected with the industry affected was afraid it was going to be injured and naturally started to howl right away. In other words because of the protection this company had they have allowed their costs to run wild. Naturally our living standards are higher here than in Great Britain and you can expect that they would be somewhat higher over here. But lately we have been concerned in this house about farming and we have been passing legislation for loans to farmers, or cash advances, as they are called. Free trade is something that would have done far more for them. Wire is not a big item as far as western farmers generally are concerned as it concerns only cattle raisers, but it illustrates the point I want to make. If they could buy such an item as wire at a cost of 90 as against a cost of 240 it would mean that wire would cost us something of the order of $5.60, provided there were no technicalities in it as to better production in this country or better technology and so on that might enter into it.

As far as freight is concerned, that would not enter into it too much because it would come into Fort Churchill for less money than if it came from down here. This kind of thing is an illustration of what an acceptance of some form of free trade with Great Britain would do for the farmer in the west. In other words, instead of giving him loans acceptance of this proposition would in many cases have doubled the purchasing power of their dollar and would be something basic that would help the farmer in the west.
Now it comes to the trade talks in the United States. For years the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he was on this side of the house said what his party would do to the United States if it could ever get hold of them and so it is interesting to read about the conference that was held by the four ministers from this government who went down to talk with their opposite numbers in the United States, particularly with reference to the wheat sales and the Are sales which that country conducted. Well now you cannot do very much business, at least satisfactory business, when you want a person to give you something if you go with the attitude-indeed nine years background of the same attitude-of hitting him over the head with a stick. It is reasonable that they got the kind of reception which they did get. As I read it in this newspaper, Sinclair Weeks, United States secretary of commerce, said at the conclusion of the United States-Canadian trade conference "We fixed 'em". Well I think that is the only concrete bit of news that came out of that conference. Since then we have had a long and rosy resume from the Minister of Finance as to what took place at the conference but at no time did he ever tell us what concessions, if any, he got. You can only conlude that Mr. Weeks was right in saying he fixed them.
Now if you go further down in this article there is another comment on the two-day conference when Mr. Weeks laughed and said that he had "certainly enjoyed his two days in the state department", and that there were in fact no United States cabinet members in attendance during the last half hour of the conference. Now this is indicative of the importance which the United States attached to this conference. They left our ministers talking to themselves for the last half hour they were there. Well I do not know how you would expect anything different if you go to beat somebody over the head in that way in order to get him to do something. It is obvious since then that this mission has done absolutely nothing because
The Address-Mr. R. Muir now the minister of agriculture for the United States, or what goes for such in that country, Mr. Benson, is now in Japan boring further into our wheat markets.
This is the record, so far, of the present government and from the standpoint of western Canada it is pretty hard to swallow. Although we may be told to have no fear because we are led by a westerner I would say that the facts so far indicate he is in the strait-jacket of Tory policy, just the same as all those before him.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) from time to time strikes stamps to commemorate certain historical events and I think perhaps something should be done with respect to striking a stamp to commemorate some of the events in the progress -and I use that word very loosely-of the Conservative party particularly. Possibly, to commemorate Sir John A. Macdonald's operations in the west we could have a stamp with a metis with a bayonet at his throat and Louis Riel hanging up on a gibbet somewhere in the background. To commemorate the regime of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett nothing could be better than the Bennett wagon running downhill.
To come back to the present administration I often think of the Minister of Finance when he sat on this side of the house and the times he used to ask the minister of agriculture of that time what the minister was going to do with the termites in the riding of Eglinton. I was concerned about that at the time because it seemed to me if you had termites boring away at the foundations of the heart of Conservative Canada in Eglinton they might spread to other parts but, having in mind the operations of this government thus far and what they might do if they had a larger majority as far as the west is concerned, I think we might well have a stamp commemorating this government which would show a termite rampant on a field of broken promises.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising for the first time in this house I would like to express my sincere congratulations to you, sir, upon your election to the high position you now hold and also the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) on his position as Deputy Speaker and I also extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) for the excellent manner in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
1018	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. R. Muir
Having started work in the coal mines of Nova Scotia at the age of 15 possibly I should feel somewhat outranked when I look around this house and find myself surrounded by lawyers, clergymen, professors, doctors and other professional men. However, I rise at this time to bring to the attention of this house the needs of my constituency and the governmental neglect which has existed in this part of Nova Scotia for many years. I would like to confine my remarks almost entirely to my own riding because of the urgency of some of the problems existing there which I think are very important and should be brought before the house. I would like to describe very briefly the constituency of Cape Breton North and Victoria which I represent and tell you something about that constituency and the problems of those who live there.
The constituency is one of three in the island of Cape Breton and it includes all of the county of Victoria and the northern section of the county of Cape Breton. In Victoria county is the community of Bad-deck, a place made famous by Alexander Graham Bell, J. A. D. MacCurdy, and others. At this point since I am talking about Cape Breton I am very happy and proud that our present Minister of External Affairs, the Hon. Sidney Smith, is a Cape Bretoner, having been born in Port Hood in the constituency which is now represented by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen). Although this constituency is represented by a Liberal member at the moment I am quite sure that will be remedied after the next election, regardless of the political speech that was made yesterday by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond.
Since we have just commemorated Remembrance Day I think it is also appropriate to mention at this time that I am very proud of the fact that on a per capita basis Cape Breton led all of Canada in the number of enlistments in the last war.
Getting back to Baddeck, it was here that the first aeroplane flight in the British empire was made. It was here that Alexander Graham Bell and F. W. "Casey" Baldwin began experimenting with the possibilities of hydrofoil craft in 1919. The original HD-4 hydrofoil is lying on the beach at Baddeck today, and I would suggest that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources look into the possibility of having this historically valuable asset taken over and preserved for future generations. It is worthy of note that our own navy is at the present time experimenting with the 1957 version of the hydrofoil 

craft named the Bras d'Or after the lakes on which Bell and Baldwin first began their experiments.
In the northern part of Victoria county is the Cape Breton highlands national park. There are no industries of any kind in this county except one or two small fish plants. There is some farming, fishing and lumbering, but not on a large scale.
The tourist industry is important to this county and it must be encouraged and developed. We have some of the finest scenery to be found in Canada but it is rather difficult for a hungry man to eat scenery, so more than the tourist industry is required if the people of Victoria county are to have even a fair measure of prosperity.
A few years ago there was a gypsum plant in operation at Dingwall and it employed in the vicinity of 100 men. This may not sound like a large operation, but nevertheless it is very important in a small community. This gypsum was, of course, shipped by water and the company concerned was obliged to pay a large amount of money to maintain the dredging that was carried out annually in the harbour from where it was shipped.
As a result, because of the exorbitant cost, the company was forced to abandon its workings there and move to another part of Nova Scotia.
Nothing has been done to maintain any breakwaters at Dingwall since 1942, except for some small concrete blocks placed on loose sand in 1954. Some weeks ago the depth of water at the entrance to Dingwall harbour was in the vicinity of six or seven feet, so that even the smallest fishing boats could not enter. I am pleased to say that, through the action of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and his staff, emergency dredging is now going on. It is questionable if this dredging is working out as successfully as we would like, but we must continue with this work so as to enable the fall and winter fishing to be carried on.
We cannot stop there. I would ask the minister and his staff to take a very serious and long look at the Dingwall situation with the thought in mind of reconstructing the north breakwater which has been allowed to deteriorate for the past 15 years without any maintenance whatsoever. I understand that installations such as are required here are carried out only when deemed feasible by the economics branch within the Department of Public Works. I feel this is a very unreasonable yardstick to use when the very existence of the many families in the area is concerned. Fishing is the only means these people have of earning a living. The question is: are we to assist them, or let them starve?

Getting back to the beginning of my remarks on the Dingwall situation; not one thing was done for these men who were thrown out of work. Those who were able to, moved out, and the balance turned to fishing, but now they will not even be able to fish if we do not provide the facilities required.
These men engaged in fishing in the Dingwall, Bay St. Lawrence, New Haven, Neils Harbour, Ingonish areas and all along the north shore of Victoria county have not been asking for charity. They have been seeking from the federal government only the normal assistance usually given by governments. By this I mean they have requested breakwaters, wharves, dredging and the like. These are not luxuries, they are the necessities of the fishing industry, but requests for installations were not granted. Either their requests were not brought before the previous government or they were ignored. I feel it is ridiculous that men in this day and age should have to go out at two or three o'clock in the morning, or at any time when a storm arises, and have to work like Roman slaves of old by pulling their boats up on the shore for protection because of lack of proper harbour facilities. In the New Haven area, a breakwater is required immediately to prevent such things as I have just mentioned. I would request the Minister of Public Works to look into this matter without delay. By the expenditure of small amounts of money, a great deal can be done for the people of these areas and I trust that it will be done in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, I have previously mentioned the national park. This is a decided asset to the constituency and it is a great attraction as far as tourists are concerned. It is also a great benefit to the people in the area as it provides employment for them. There is one very important question which I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), namely that wages paid to those who are working there are less than those paid for the same work done in other parts of Canada. As I understand it the rate of wages paid is governed by what is known as the prevailing rate. In the areas to which I refer there are no known standards of what is the prevailing rate because there is no industry there. In any event, I believe it is wholly wrong to pay less in Nova Scotia than elsewhere.
I cannot find any justification whatsoever for the federal government paying higher wages for the same job of work in one part of Canada than it does in another. Furthermore, if equal rates of pay were provided for
The Address-Mr. R. Muir similar work no matter where such work was done it would tend to increase the general wage level and so bring it into line with that paid in other parts of the country where better wages are paid. Those in the civil service receive the same salaries no matter where they work; a civil servant working in Cape Breton, for example, does not receive less because the general wage rate in the district is less than it is elsewhere, and the same should apply to those who are working in the national park.
There are several other matters I should like to mention with regard to the park. For instance, there is a great lack of suitable camping grounds, and this shortage has become a decided problem in the past few years. Camping has increased around 200 per cent I would say in recent years, and the net result has been a very serious shortage of camping areas, toilet and laundry facilities. Another problem is the need for recreational centres where movies, lectures and other forms of entertainment may be enjoyed after the daylight hours or in rainy weather.
Then, again, the highway in the park between Ingonish and Neils Harbour is very narrow and very dangerous. I feel this highway should be widened considerably and the dangerous curves removed. I should like also to recommend a program of street lighting within the park in the immediate park area. Consideration should be given, also, to the construction of a new golf club house. The present building is a converted barn and it still looks like a barn.
These suggested improvements may not, perhaps, help the residents of the area very greatly but I feel they would provide the residents of Victoria county with a certain amount of employment which is urgently required.
The Cape Breton north section of the constituency is partly rural and partly industrialized. There are two large coal mines owned by the old Sydney Collieries Limited of Dosco and some smaller mines operated by independent operators. As hon. members are fully aware conditions have not been good in the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia for quite a number of years. Competition from other sources of fuel, loss of markets to oil, loss of traditional sales to the Canadian National Railways as a result of the changeover to diesel engines in the Atlantic region have all had their effects and it has been very difficult for the industry to overcome them. A determined effort has been made by employers and employees, men and management, to bring down the cost of production. Mines have been mechanized and modernized so that the unit cost of

The Address-Mr. R. Muir production could be lowered. Some mines have been closed. It is sad to say that some of those mines were in communities where mining was the only source of employment. The whole economy of such communities has been wrecked and their welfare gravely threatened.
The cost of producing coal can be lowered only so far; there is a definite limit beyond which it is not possible to go. This is true especially in Cape Breton coal fields where most of the coal is mined under the sea. In fact, there are some instances where they go five miles under the water. Experts tell us that coal will again be in great demand in about 10 years, if the industry can survive that long. It needs markets, immediate markets, and many of us believe that such markets can be found, or at least partly found, in the maritime provinces by the use of coal to produce power. Cheap power is needed in the maritime provinces. In order to produce cheap power from coal there must be cheap coal and that is not possible without assistance.
The assistance we ask for is to have the coal subvention policy extended so that subventions would be paid on the movement of coal within the maritime provinces when such coal is used to produce power. This would give immediate assistance to the industry and it would also assist in the development of cheap power in the maritime provinces.
Having, shall I say, Mr. Speaker, a rough idea of what the coal miners' problems are, and the dangers they have to face daily,
I do not hesitate to recommend to the government that they are deserving of every consideration that can be given by this government. Without such assistance there is grave danger that the mining industry of Nova Scotia will be no more.
While I. am on the subject of coal I should like to bring to the attention of the government a matter of prime importance, not only to the coal miners of my constituency but to all the coal miners in the province of Nova Scotia. As the dominion coal board is comprised at the present time labour does not have any representation on this important body. I would suggest to the government that they give immediate consideration to this oversight and appoint a member to this board from within the ranks of the United Mine Workers of America in which all the miners of Nova Scotia are organized. Then labour would be truly represented on the coal board.
Another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the government is the town of Sydney Mines. Here we have an un-

employment insurance office that has always been a suboffice of the main one at Sydney. This causes considerable delay in processing claims and it has many other objectionable features. I feel that the Sydney Mines office should be separate from, and independent of Sydney altogether. Then, of course, the people of Victoria county could also use this office. As it is now they have to travel many miles farther to Sydney. The office is located upstairs in a building that is over 50 years old and looks it. This creates a hardship on our older citizens who have to climb several flights of stairs to file their claims. I think the time is long past when we should have a new federal building at Sydney Mines that would house the aforementioned office, the post office and other governmental departments.
Also in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, is the town of North Sydney. This is a very important seaport. It is also the Canadian National terminus for Newfoundland. Canadian National ships ply between here and Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, and the well and famously-known William Carson sails between North Sydney and Argentia. After Newfoundland entered confederation there was a greatly increased business between North Sydney and Newfoundland. To take care of it a new wharf was built and modern facilities were provided. It was felt at that time that the new pier would be able to handle the business for many years to come and that the pier formerly used by the Canadian National Railways could be used as a public wharf. However, the business has already outgrown the new pier and the C.N.R. must use both the old and new wharves. This is a very happy situation, but it means that the facilities of the C.N.R. must be expanded and a new public wharf is required for North Sydney.
With a new wharf it is expected there will be a great increase in business, as already ships have had to be diverted from this port for lack of space. Others have had to wait until a berth was available. For example, last year saw 1,290 ships, representing 16 nations and aggregating 2.25 million tons, being piloted into North Sydney harbour waters and had proper facilities been available that figure would have been higher. I think we should give every encouragement to shipping as it means a great deal to the town in general as well as to the commerce of Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that the Minister of Public Works and his department have within the past two months

ti-Ken some concrete steps toward the erection of the long-talked-about federal building at North Sydney. I would suggest to the minister that plans for this long-awaited building be proceeded with just as soon as possible.
A matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the government is the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, as passed by this house on June 27, 1955. This legislation, as I understand it, was designed to assist fishermen engaged in a primary fishing enterprise. As it now reads, it is definitely not benefiting the fishermen in my constituency to any appreciable degree, or in fact in any other area of Canada. An example of its ineffectiveness is that since this act was made law only 40 loans totalling approximately $41,000 have been granted to the fishermen of Nova Scotia and the figures for Newfoundland are even less impressive. I feel the reason for this is that the regulations are so stringent that the act is rendered ineffective and impractical. In plain every-day language, there is too much red tape connected with it. I would urge the government to make an immediate re-appraisal of this legislation and amend it so that it will do the job that was originally intended for it.
In my constituency, Mr. Speaker, we also have the Point Edward naval base, which contributes greatly to the economic life of the surrounding areas. A matter that I should like the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) to take particular note of is the fact that this base is not being utilized to the degree of which it is capable. At the present time they are busily engaged at the base in refitting and preparing some Bangor minesweepers which are shortly to be turned over to the Turkish government under the mutual-aid program. After that is a large question mark. There are no other prospects in sight. This is unfortunate because at the Point Edward naval base we have the workmen, the technicians and the equipment to refit ships up to and as large as the tribal class destroyer. All that is required is that some of these ships find their way to Point Edward.
May I also suggest to the minister that he ?ive serious consideration to the basing of a ninesweeper flotilla at Point Edward. This laval base has proven its worth in regard to rorth Atlantic defence in the past and is still of vital importance in the north At-antic defence scheme.
I should like to serve notice on this gov-;rnment that the people of the constituency )f Cape Breton North and Victoria have been eft out in the cold for such a long, long ;ime that they are going to require a great
The Address-Mr. R. Muir deal of attention to warm them up. In Nova Scotia we feel and we know that we have not shared in the growth and prosperity of the rest of Canada. Our people are not as well off; they do not have the opportunity for employment that appears to be available elsewhere.
This is one of the reasons why the increases in old age security and other benefits recently announced are of great importance to Nova Scotia. It is very welcome. It will give much needed assistance to those who require it most. The government is indeed to be commended for their attitude in this matter. This government, Mr. Speaker, has been in office only a few months but it has already demonstrated its worth. It is attacking the problems of our country with courage and ability. It has the support of the people of Nova Scotia and will have, I am sure, for a long time to come.
Finally, I should like to comment briefly on certain remarks that have been made in the house. I listened very attentively to the speech today of the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). I will not comment further than to say that possibly he should endeavour to get the opportunity to try out for the cast of "My Fur Lady", which has been seen in the city recently.
As a newcomer I certainly expected that there would be a certain amount of politicking, if I am allowed to use that word, and I expected that it would be done by all parties. Of course, one thing I am very happy to see is that some of the Liberal members from the maritimes after many years of silence have realized their responsibilities and have finally decided to open their mouths on behalf of the maritimes. This is a very good thing and I hope that in the future they will join with us in securing for the maritimes the rights these provinces so richly deserve.
One observation I did make was that during the debate on the wheat bill the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart)-I am sorry he is not here-for reasons known only to himself tried to pit one province against another, one section of the country against another. That was his own idea and I do not know why he did it. Of course, it has been impressed upon my mind since I have been here that it appears to be one of the policies of the Liberal party to divide and conquer, whether it be a case of province against province, religion against religion or race against race. No matter what it is, that would appear to be their aim, as was so aptly portrayed by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). In his emotional outburst he did his best to try to promote disunity in this great country of ours.

It is my intention to devote the major portion of my address to what I consider the most striking problem confronting Canada today, the labour situation. Before doing so, however, I feel I am somewhat duty bound and I also desire to let hon. members know something about my constituency and what is expected to take place in that area next year. As hon. members are probably aware, British Columbia will be celebrating its centennial in 1958. In my constituency of New Westminster we are very fortunate indeed to have the first and second capitals of British Columbia. The first is a district known as Fort Langley.
The former federal government and the provincial government, in co-operation with the municipal authorities and the native sons of the district, have seen fit to restore the fort and I understand that Princess Margaret has been invited to officiate at the official opening of the fort some time next year. I suggest that all members of the house, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the other members of the cabinet, would benefit by being present and taking part in the historic events upon that occasion.
I heard one member today tell us about the difficult tasks that the Prime Minister has to perform in the course of his duties and the rigid schedule which he is trying to follow. I agree with that hon. member, but in looking at today's Ottawa Journal I see a picture of the Prime Minister greeting Miss Canada and I suggest that possibly there are a good number of the junior representatives of his party in the house who would be only too happy to take over that particular task from him. It is the kind of job that possibly might be allocated to some of the other members.
Fort Langley, as I said, was the first capital of British Columbia. It is the centre of fishing and agricultural industries and today is undergoing a considerable industrial awakening. The second capital of British Columbia was the city of New Westminster, and it too is preparing to take part in the 1958 pageant marking the centennial year of our province. New Westminster is the home of British Columbia's first regiment. I consider it very unfortunate indeed that this government has not seen fit to give it the recognition it deserves.

This is possibly one of the most concentrated industrial and commercial areas within Canada. At the moment we are suffering somewhat from conditions which are making themselves more and more apparent in the way of unemployment and a lag in industrial development by reason of the policies followed by this government. However, I am satisfied that if you, sir, or any other member of this parliament should see fit to make his way to New Westminster you will be delighted with the reception you receive. We are proud of the two newer cities in our area, the cities of Langley and White Rock having been incorporated within the last two years.
One of our difficult problems is connected with the Fraser river. The river itself is a navigable stream and was declared such by a previous administration. It is being used a great deal but not to the extent it should be. The fact is that navigation is not as freely and easily conducted as it might be, but we are hoping that this government will see the light and some change in policy in respect of river development will take place.
We have another problem connected with the river. It has to do with fishing. This problem has been drawn to the attention of the Department of Fisheries. It has particularly to do with the opening of the Fraser river above the Pattullo bridge and as far as the Mission bridge to the fishing industry. The former government saw fit to close this area to fishing, but we are hopeful this administration will see the merit of reopening it, not only from the viewpoint of saving dollars for the fishermen but also :o help the community as a whole.
River crossings, of course, play a major part in our development, and we have major problems arising from the fact. The former government was very adamant in its attitude oward giving assistance to these river :rossings. We are hopeful that this govern-nent may see that a change is desirable. Dne of the leftovers we have from the former idministration is the Langley airport. This lirport, although started many years ago, las had to exist and to grow by being built ip with the leftovers from other airports vhich did not require expenditures upon hem. The result is that today the airport, tlthough playing a major role in the develop-nent of agriculture and industry, is certainly n need of assistance. The present government has not indicated it intends to change he policy with respect to this airport, but
would suggest that they make a careful eview of the situation to see what can be lone.

In so far as harbour maintenance is concerned, I have heard a great deal about what the Conservatives inherited as a legacy from the former administration in the way of waste, extravagance and inefficiency. However, it is remarkable to me to note that this government seems to be carrying on the identical program of the former administration, which would indicate that this government is still not aware of the changes that have to take place. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) advise the house, in response to my question, that the government diking program has been changed. This will ease the problem of many municipalities in this respect.
In so far as the shipping industry is concerned naturally, having one of the main ports in Canada in the city of New Westminster, I am interested in discovering exactly what advance the present government is making in the way of establishing a shipping fleet for Canada. I took particular note of the action announced yesterday with respect to the transfer of our east coast fleet to Trinidad.
The main industry in the area is lumbering. Sales are down and the industry is suffering from problems that are common to the industry as a whole in Canada. I will not go into detail at this time in so far as those problems are concerned.
In so far as transportation is concerned, we have the Canadian National shops which, of course, do present certain problems which are not unlike those the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has raised so often in this house. This area does have an agricultural section, and we are still in need of the extension of the P.F.R.A. to British Columbia, or at least some assistance similar to it. We do have other problems, too, related to freight assistance on feed grains. At this point I wish to compliment the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and congratulate him upon the prompt action he and his government saw fit to take in assisting the turkey raisers, after hearing recommendations from me and interviewing the turkey raisers themselves. I recognize that this assistance is only temporary, but it is a step in the right direction of meeting a problem when it arises.
This brings me to the main problem which faces my area at this particular moment. I speak of the question of unemployment. Recently the Prime Minister made a statement which caused me a good deal of concern. What he said has been carried by many newspapers throughout the country.

The Address-Mr. Hahn The Montreal Gazette of November 9 carried a very lucid account of this particular statement. The article reads, in part:
"It seems clear," he added, "that the strategy of the high command of the Liberal party is to spread fear and gloom and preach doom and to pretend that where unemployment exists this (Progressive Conservative) government is to blame."
. . . "there has been a levelling off during the last year and a half."
I am very pleased to hear there is a levelling off of the unemployment situation. I hope that the figures we have today will indicate that the levelling off period has been completed. However, I do not believe the government is facing the facts. The fact of the matter is that we do have unemployment in Canada today. It is true, as the Prime Minister has suggested in this article, and in some of his statements, that we have more people employed in Canada today than probably at any other time. But it is also a recognized fact that if we have more than 1 per cent or 2 per cent of our labouring force unemployed then we have above the point usually allowed for transitional employees, that is, those who go from one job to the next.
I am rather disturbed when the Prime Minister of this country tries to shrug off a situation in which unemployment in this country has increased to such an extent that it causes a great number of industrialists and a great number of labourers a great deal of concern. Yet, the Prime Minister tells us we should not worry. In this article the Prime Minister goes on to say:
"Criticism is of the essence in our system," he said. "But the sowing of fear of mass unemployment is a dangerous course to follow, for it can lead to a depression complex whether so intended or not."
I must agree with what the Prime Minister has to say in respect of a fear complex. However, facing reality does not mean necessarily that one is trying to inject fear into the people. This is a matter of facing the facts. As I read this article I wondered whether this was a deliberate attempt on the part of the Prime Minister-I do not believe it was but it might be interpreted as such-to coerce and to prevent the members of parliament from bringing this particular matter to the attention of the people as a whole.
We are faced with a problem that industrialists, members of parliament and governments at all levels must take hold of at this time and examine into. I ask this question. How long are we to wait before be decide that conditions are of such a grave

nature that we are expected to say something to the people about them? When is the government going to become aware of it? Or must I wait until my constituents write to me about it before I have anything to say in respect of the matter?
I do not care a hoot whether the Prime Minister inherited this problem from the Conservatives or whether he inherited it from the Liberals. The fact of the matter is that many thousands of people are unemployed in New Westminster riding and in Canada and I am concerned about those particular people. My main interest is in knowing what is going to be done about it. As I say, men and women are out of work by the thousands. What is this parliament prepared to do? What is labour prepared to do? What is industry prepared to do? This is not a time for us to wear a blindfold. It is the time for us to be alert to the problem that faces this country and to try to do something about it.
Political parties throughout this country- that means in particular C.C.F.'ers, Liberals, Conservatives or Social Crediters-have all indicated that we are quite prepared to sit down with this government to see whether or not we can resolve the problems that face the nation today. It is with that fact in mind that I speak, namely that this government has a greater degree of co-operation than any government hitherto has ever had in that respect. There is no one rising in this house for the purpose of opposition just for the sake of opposition alone. They are here for only one purpose and that is to bring to the attention of the government a solution to the problem or at least a solution that we think might be desirable and one that we could use.

Things have not changed from the

good old days of the Liberals. You present a suggestion, you wire them, you explain it to them and yet you still wait for their reply.

We must keep these industries in operation. It is most important to the economy of Canada and more particularly to the economy of the district in which they might be located.
What are the facts in respect of unemployment. I am not blaming the government particularly, or not just this government. It is a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, that possibly the Bank of Canada is as much to blame as anyone. Of those at present seeking work 27 per cent are from outside the New Westminster and Fraser valley areas, the highest percentage yet recorded,-
That, sir, was what gave me cause to rise in my place on October 31 and ask a question of the Minister of Labour. At that time I asked him this question as reported at page 598 of Hansard:
What consideration, if any, is the government giving to the suggestion to the unemployed that they would be well advised to remain in the community in which they now live unless directed to some other labour field in the Canadian market by the officers of the unemployment insurance commission?
The minister very kindly replied as follows:
In the first place the government, or the unemployment insurance commission in this case, is hardly in a position to suggest to an individual who is interested in finding work that he should remain in a locality where he cannot get employment. People will insist on remaining free to look for work wherever it may be found.
That is true and I would agree with him that they insist on that. But certainly this government could direct them and could say that it is bad business to go into an area today where we have too many people at the present time who are looking for work.
Potentially we believe that we might expect a great number more of unemployed. Not too long ago I believe the Canadian Labour Congress rather indicated that they expected some 750,000 people to be unemployed this winter. In the Ottawa Citizen of November 8 I find it says that a qualified government official predicted that unemployment this winter will likely hit 750,000, the highest figure since the end of the second world war. Yet we are supposed to show no concern over the fact that we have in the Canadian Congress of Labour men and women who are interested in the labour field indicating

The Address-Mr. Hahn that they expect an all-time high in unemployment. At the same time qualified government officials indicate they expect an alltime high in unemployment and we are advised that we should not show the natural interest in this matter which I think we have a right to show and are indeed expected to show.
Now the reasoning is wrong. This question must be resolved. The only place it can be resolved is in the parliament of Canada. That is why we are here and that is what we are supposed to do. We should assist the government in taking care of these matters and I think we are all quite prepared to do so; I know we as a party are and I am convinced that others are too. I have many other clippings I could read but my time is running out very rapidly. Well at any rate the article goes on to use unnecessarily harsh words about the Prime Minister which I do not feel add anything to the discussion and so I will not put them on the record. However, further down it says:
And the prospect of large-scale unemployment this winter has been tacitly admitted by the government, which has taken steps to try to reduce it. For one thing, it has cut down immigration (a mistaken policy, in this newspaper's opinion, but that is another matter). For another, it has made $150 million available at low interest rates for low-cost housing.
Well these may be cures, but the article goes on to say:
And jobs don't depend on public debate: they depend on export markets, inflation, population growth, and similar factors.
This is possibly a condition which this government did inherit from the Liberals, the fact we did not have export markets, and it is something which some of the hon. members of this house tried to do something about a year ago, namely early in the spring when the other administration was in office.

We asked them to see to it that they traded and accepted sterling either bloc or convertible-or inconvertible for that matter- and see to it that they opened up channels of trade one way or another. However as usual such was not the case.
This article goes on to say:
It is up to the government to give a lead on this issue,
It is up to the parliament to do something about it. Hon. members may consider that because 1 was quoting from the Ottawa Citizen I was using a somewhat biased newspaper but I have a clipping from a Vancouver paper which British Columbia members would recognize as the official organ of the Conservative party; it has this to say:
What we call our "way of life" in western societies is now under test as never before.
This article appeared on November 5, 1957 and the way of life referred to of course is our way of life as compared with the communist way of life. It goes on:
The internal threat is less clearly identified because it is composed of a number of things. The test of western society's fitness to survive will rest on the realism and courage with which it faces up to, and finds solutions for, its own weaknesses.
We must find a solution to our own weaknesses and unemployment is a weakness which has been with us since the early thirties and a long time before that and if democratic society is to exist and continue to exist it is our responsibilty to see to it that we do not have unemployment. I read on:
If during an era when the communist system is forging ahead, with its working force straining to keep up with productive demands, our society fails to keep its own people usefully employed, this will be a most dangerous failure.
Though the communist system may prove to be one of the greatest let-down's in history, the fact will not help us if our system becomes embroiled in internal difficulties for which many will not be able to see any rational reason.
You cannot rationalize with a person who is unemployed, who has no job and has not a full bread box. You can understand only too well, as should this government, how difficult it is to try to convince these people that this thing must be, that we should have unemployment regularly. I beseech you, sir, to advise the government-well it is not your position to do so, I recognize that-but through you I would request the government to give further attention to this particular question.
The reason the communist government is as strong as it is today is because of happy men and contented men who not only have their stomach full but have jobs as well. They do have jobs, whether they are forced to do them by slave labour or not-I am not here to argue at this time. That is one of

the reasons they are a happy and contented lot, in so far as one can be happy and contented under slavery. Therein lies the strength of communism and if we are going to fight it we will have to fight it by looking after our own backyard and seeing to it that the people of this country are fully employed.
The Vancouver and district labour council wrote to I think all the members from British Columbia submitting the problem in so far as they were concerned. I have with me the letter addressed to myself dated November 8, 1957 requesting that I attend a meeting. It says:
The purpose of the meeting is to discuss ways and means of alleviating unemployment which is prevalent in this area at the present time, and is increasing daily at an alarming rate. Predictions are that it will reach an all-time high very soon unless people in authority, together with industry, take steps immediately to provide work for those unemployed.
Now we are told by this government that conditions are not too bad and that we are spreading a fear complex if we continue in this vein. Certainly labour itself recognizes the problem and I say that we should see to it that we recognize it also. The city of Vancouver, I read from a news item of Tuesday, November 5, says this:
Vancouver's appeals to the senior governments for public projects to fight unemployment will be meaningless if voters turn down the city's five-year plan in December.
Now the city of Vancouver is trying to keep its men and women in work and therein lies another problem. The premier of my own province had this to say, and I now read from a news clipping also of November 5:
Premier Bennett proposed Monday that if the Bank of Canada did not heed Finance Minister Donald Fleming's opposition to tight money, "it be reorganized immediately".
I am sure our good friend from Westmorland (Mr. Murphy), who seems to be out of his element in his own party because they brought on this tight money policy if I understand correctly, will appreciate this.

I know, as everyone in this house knows, that the present government has had only a period of five months in which to do these things and I recognize that the government is a new government and has to be established as such; it has not had experience for 22 years. Nevertheless, the problems raised in this house having been drawn to its attention so frequently I think it is high time something was done about them.
I have only one request to make in conclusion, and that is that we put Canada first. All political parties have declared that they will co-operate, and they have indicated in this house that they would do so. Let us, therefore, put Canada first and get the people back to work.

Mr. Speaker, it is with legitimate pride and great humility that I rise to make my maiden speech in this distinguished house and to represent my fellow Canadians in Trinity riding by speaking in this debate in reply to the speech from the throne delivered by Her Gracious Majesty the Queen at the memorable opening of this twenty-third parliament of Canada.
As I apply myself to the discharge of my responsibilities I should like first to express my gratitude to the electors of Trinity for having chosen me as their representative the only Liberal from Toronto in this House of Commons-and I pray that I may always serve this chamber, my constituents and fellow Canadians with loyalty and devotion. I am honoured to be associated in this house with five of my colleagues in the medical profession, and with the first Italian and the first Chinese Canadians to sit in this house, and I believe I experience some of their emotions because I happen to be the first Canadian of Polish descent to be elected to the House of Commons.

The Address-Mr. Haidasz
May I congratulate the Speaker of the House of Commons upon his election to this high office and responsibility. I offer him my sincere support and co-operation. To you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, I extend my sincere felicitations and offer true co-operation. May I also congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for their fine performances.
I confess I deeply regret that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) has announced his intention to resign his post for reasons of health. Along with the rest of the Canadian public I have admired his firmness, dignity and devotion to duty which enabled the Liberal government to give Canada the greatest measure of national unity, full nationhood, international standing and unprecedented economic prosperity. That is why I am proud to be associated with this great Canadian party of reform under the guidance of the present Leader of the Opposition who now takes his place in Canadian history alongside Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir John A. Macdonald.
I am proud to belong to Canada's one and only truly national party. Let me remind hon. members opposite that it was the Liberal party which obtained the largest majority of votes in the last election. I must also confess that I was scandalized to hear from my colleagues on this side of the house that the Tory party had one set of election promises for the people of the province of Quebec and a totally different one for the people of the province of Ontario.

I am also sorry that the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) should have been placed in the position of a two-faced politician by his colleagues, for in Toronto he had to say one thing last week, and four months ago he had to say a totally different thing to the people in Three Rivers.
And now, Mr. Speaker, as is the custom, I should like to acquaint especially the newcomers to this house with the particular features of Trinity and the needs of its constituents which were so ably served by distinguished members who have preceded me such as Hugh Plaxton, Senator Arthur Roebuck, the late Lionel Conacher and Donald Carrick.
Trinity is located in the southwestern sector of the great metropolis of Toronto. The southern limit of my riding borders on lake Ontario and the Toronto harbour. The armouries, Fort York, and the world-renowned park of the Canadian national

exhibition occupy the southern portion along with the great industries of Massey-Harris and John Inglis.
The dependable industrious, and public-spirited residents of Trinity represent the most complete cross-section of any Canadian metropolis. The stalwart Anglo-Saxons and Irish comprise the majority of its population, followed by the Italians, the Poles, the Jewish, Ukranians, Slovaks, Lithuanians, Czechs and many others. Among these there is also an active group of people from the West Indies federation which I hope will soon join us in the family of sovereign nations, the British commonwealth. The rich traditions and the cultures one thousand years old or more and the firsthand experiences in the struggle against communist tyranny of many of these newcomers to freedom-loving Canada have already contributed and will continue to contribute immeasurably to the stature of this great country. This enviable mosaic, composed of different sizes, shapes and colours is, may I assure you, strongly cemented not only by a common allegiance to the crown and a common Canadian citizenship but also by convictions of loyalty, pride and faith in the past, present and future of Canada.
At this point in my address may I pay tribute to the first Polish immigrant to become a citizen of Toronto 100 years ago, an engineer who built so many railroads, highways and bridges in Ontario that he was elevated to knighthood by Queen Victoria. The name of this man, who worked and resided in Trinity riding and who contributed so much to the development of Toronto and Ontario was Sir Casimir Gzowski. The city council of Toronto paid tribute to his memory last year by naming a park in his honour.
Another new Canadian who contributed to the development of this country is Stephen Roman, a Slovak immigrant, who came to this great land of opportunity less than 20 years ago with only a few dollars in his pocket, but who by hard work and brain power formed, among other companies, the world's largest uranium mine, the Consolidated Denison Mines of which he is president. That is why at this point I pay tribute to the wise and courageous policy of immigration of Mackenzie King, a policy vigorously and successfully carried out by the former minister of immigration, Mr. Harris, and by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
Since it is the duty of a loyal opposition to oppose, I cannot see how one can offer effective opposition without constructive

criticism. Yet, I very well know that in many minds political criticism is today frequently regarded as an ugly word, conjuring up pictures of insidious radicals and non-conformists. And before we realize it political criticism can become regarded as an unCanadian activity instead of democracy's greatest safeguard.
Nowhere in the world more ardently than in the Kremlin is the critic considered a conspirator and as one deserving of exile and frequently death. That is why communist Kremlin, believing itself to be infallible, and determined to revolutionize this world into a godless communist society, continues in the minds of free men to be intolerant and intolerable. In the western civilization, the traditional attitude is that criticism is an attempt to test whether what is, might not be better.
Edmund Burke once said that "a nation without means of reform is without means of survival", and I personally believe that no reform can be achieved in a truly free democratic state without honest and vigorous criticism. Therefore, it is my ardent hope that this government will never resent criticism.
The city council and the citizens of Toronto expect great things from this government, and this hope is based upon the election promises of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and upon the very close friendship and co-operation which now exist between the Prime Minister of Canada, the premier of Ontario and the super-mayor of metropolitan Toronto, who sat together in the front row in Massey hall on that memorable day of April 25, 1957, at the opening of the Conservative election campaign.
At last the taxpayers of Toronto, burdened with municipal taxes steadily rising to intolerable levels, will get relief if only these election promises are all kept. Toronto has been expanding so rapidly that the taxes levied on its home-owners have become an unjust burden because they have to pay for municipal services that were basically the responsibility of the provincial and federal governments.
Education, the building of schools, the relief of the indigent and the vast number of unemployed, the building of hospitals, slum clearance, subsidization of low-cost housing, the administration of justice, the building of roadways and freeways and safer railway crossings should be met also by the provincial and federal governments. Furthermore, many responsible Torontonians are alarmed at the nonchalant attitude and delays of certain levels of government in refusing to start financing the projects of the Metropolitan

The Address-Mr. Haidasz Toronto Conservation Authority in order to remove the dangers of the Humber and Don river valleys which, during hurricane "Hazel" took the lives of 81 of our citizens.
In this address I consider it a pleasant duty to defend also the interests of the small businessman of whom there are over 2,000 in Trinity and who are hard pressed and heading for bankruptcy owing to the greedy expansion of giant chain stores. The present Prime Minister, in his opening campaign speech in Toronto last April, stated that the Tories will undertake to set up a committee composed of members of the cabinet and representatives of small business associations from all of Canada to take necessary effective action to assist small business, the backbone of our national business. May I remind the Prime Minister that he has done nothing and forecast nothing about this election promise.
1 also urge the present government to change the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase benefits from 31 to 52 weeks for the unemployed and also to eliminate waiting periods for payments, as was promised in Toronto and other parts of Canada during his election campaign.
When I voted for the $9 increase for the senior citizens I did not forget to remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) of the promise of his government to include an escalator clause to protect this $9 rise against the rising cost of living and to gear it to the national productivity. I reminded him during that debate that the senior citizens, depending solely on the old age pension of $55, have barely enough for three nutritious meals for 30 days. Where are those poor people who depend solely on the old age pension to get the money for shelter, clothing and other essential hygienic products to lead a decent life? That is why I urge this government to use their influence on Premier Frost to be more just and to be even generous in his province's share to care for those destitute senior citizens.
In my riding of Trinity I have over 1,000 old age pensioners in homes for the aged such as Lambert Lodge and Hilltop Acres. I was horrified last summer when metropolitan Toronto took from those old age pensioners $5 out of their $6 increase, which is a very unjust act for I believe that all of us in this House of Commons, when we vote for an increase for these old age pensioners we believe that that increase belongs to them and is not intended to reimburse municipalities for their obligation to our destitute senior citizens.
During my varied experience as a practitioner of medicine among the working class, the poor and the aged in Toronto, and mostly

The Address-Mr. Haidasz in my riding of Trinity, I have become intimately aware of and particularly concerned with the medical needs and the social welfare of my constituents and that is why I regret that in the speech from the throne there was no mention whatsoever of hospital insurance and diagnostic services. The advances of medicine in alleviating suffering and preventing disease were steadily made available to all Canadians by the progressive and beneficial assistance of the national health plans of the previous government. Federal grants to hospitals, co-operation in the production of Salk vaccine, numerous other services and a variety of pensions brought substantial relief to a wide sector of our citizens. The immediate availability of the benefits of the National Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act can provide considerable relief in the cost of sickness. Credit is due to the members of the 22nd parliament for passing unanimously this most significant piece of social welfare legislation and, above all, to the distinguished former minister of national health and welfare whose tireless energy and persistent determination made this dream come true.
I join with those who regret that the Ontario hospital commission will not provide these benefits prior to January 1, 1959 and that, as recently announced, this commission has disallowed outpatient diagnostic and laboratory services which federal legislation, enacted on April 12, 1957, so generously provided.
I therefore respectfully appeal to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to use his influence on the Ontario government to bring these benefits to our ailing citizens earlier and in a fuller measure. There are many other health problems whose solutions are urgently needed-and I draw them to the attention of the minister-such as mental health research and the modern care of the mentally ill, cancer research, research into chronic diseases such as heart disease, arthritis, blindness problems and especially helping to set up glaucoma clinics and banks for corneal transplant tissues, infant and maternal mortality, dental decay, alcoholism, increasing highway traffic deaths which are occurring every summer on our highways and many other medical problems.
I also support every effort of the provincial and federal health departments to ban the indiscriminate sale of tranquilizing drugs and to order their use only upon the recommendation of the patient's physician.
To solve these problems we need more hospitals, more research workers, more doctors,

nurses and technicians. The existing shortage of personnel demands a more vigorous program of education and specialized training.
Never before has our way of life demanded so much scientific education as now and yet, unfortunately, Canada today is in a situation unique in her history. Never before have there been so few in the age group 15 to 25 years in proportion to those in other decennial age groups. This has been brought about by the low birth rate in the 1930's. Moreover, emigration to the United States of our university graduates and skilled workers has long been heavy.
Another contributing factor to this shortage, and especially to the shortage of teachers and professors, is the recent clamping down on migration of teachers, professors and other skilled workers from the countries of central Europe to Canada. It might be interesting to note that of every 100 children in Canada who start school only seven enter a university and only five obtain a degree, and very few of these ever become scientists.
Among other causes of this dearth of scientists, engineers and teachers are the poor salaries for professors, lack of funds, insufficient incentive, decline of prestige of educated people and increasing numbers of self-satisfied citizens who seem quite certain that everything desirable in life is to be found in a ranch style bungalow, a television set, travel and convivial gatherings. These people are avid for the products of science, particularly in medicine and entertainment, but they feel no attraction for a life dedicated to intellectual discipline nor for scientists as personalities.
Now that the very material things in which most people put their trust are in jeopardy Canada and the western world are faced with a need for scientists. An editorial in a Canadian weekly magazine of contemporary affairs remarked last month that "Sputnick is a symbol not so much of Russian superiority as of the failure of American and Canadian education". A NATO committee reported last month that the Soviet union is graduating nearly twice as many scientists on a per capita basis as the NATO countries put together and is also accelerating her output rate.
The need for scientists in Canada was forecast at a conference on scientific and technical manpower at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, in September, 1956. It was stated there that by 1980 Canada must quadruple her currently employed 40,000 engineers, probably more than quadruple today's scientist force of 20,000 and produce ten times as many technicians and have

55,000 university teachers. These fabulous figures are most alarming. In Canada there have been cries of alarm and some talk from the leaders of the present government, but the fears and suggestions of Canada's research directors and scientists warn us that the government is hindering the progress of scientific research by ordering cuts in expenditures.
In spite of the appeals for aid for scientific research and in spite of the election promises by Conservative party candidates of federal grants for education, these same people ignored in the throne speech the urgent need for such aid and ignored mentioning any federal grants to our universities which constitute our very first line of defence. I am sure many members and many Canadians were humiliated and scandalized as I was that Dr. Norman MacKenzie, president of the University of British Columbia has just returned from a tour of the United States to beg United States industrialists to give donations to Canadian universities and colleges.
I urge the government that this session of parliament should not close without granting financial aid to our universities and without giving grants to aid needy but talented students. Recently Walter Gordon, of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, stated that learning should receive economic help even if this meant we could not spend quite as much on other things. I would also recommend the formation of a national education and research committee to advise governments and universities and to solicit financial aid from governments, industries and private benefactors. I highly commend my colleague on this side of the house, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) for proposing the following resolution which appeared on the opening day of parliament:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so as to provide for the exemption from income taxes of tuition fees paid to universities-
He also included other schools of higher learning.
-as well as the costs to students o fall textbooks and scientific equipment-
We can assist our universities tremendously by introducing more liberal changes in our tax laws to encourage corporations to donate more money toward educational purposes such as to expand university facilities, provide more teachers and scientists, increase professors' salaries and promote scientific research, both pure and applied. More money should be available for scholarships, bursaries and loan 96698-66J
The Address-Mr. Haidasz funds even at high school level as well as at college and post-graduate levels in order to identify, encourage and support our young Canadians who have the incentive and aptitude to profit by advanced training. Industry and government could also help students help themselves by providing more summer employment and by exempting these students from unemployment insurance pay deductions. The provision of facilities to expand our universities and to provide bursaries for teachers to take summer courses would also help our drive to promote scientific advancement and produce more teachers.
Education and scientific research are the foundation of our national strength which will serve to increase our international stature and serve as a strong factor in the preservation of security and freedom. In order to preserve peace and freedom and, above all, to check the threat of communism which subordinates its peoples and policies in order to achieve its goal of world domination, we must reappraise our standards. The danger and tragedy of the progressive march of communism and the ruthless extirpation by communist dictators of freedom and basic human rights in peace-loving countries such as Hungary, Poland, the Ukraine, East Germany, the Baltic states and the Balkan countries is most appalling. A few weeks ago we marked the first anniversary of the uprisings in Hungary and Poland against their oppressors. By resisting communist tyranny with heavy personal sacrifice these people undermined the progress of communism and helped our western world in the fight against this godless and ruthless force.
The Liberal government may well be proud of its contribution of economic aid and swift emergency immigration measures to assist refugees from those areas, an act which proved that Canada backs her words with concrete action and which raised our country's stature in the eyes of the free world.
It was indeed fortifying to hear Her Majesty state that the ministers of the present government will do their utmost to participate in NATO and the United Nations in order to preserve peace. We are hopeful that the meeting of the fifteen NATO heads will determine definite and workable plans to enable co-operation in the pooling of scientific knowledge, co-ordination of defence and the extension of economic and cultural assistance to the countries that are in need.
By working through the United Nations, just one year ago the former secretary of state for external affairs was able to divert the dangerous course of the Suez crisis. This achievement in diplomacy in the United

The Address-Mr. Haidasz Nations' forum won him the Nobel Peace Prize, bringing distinction and honour to himself, his party, to this house and to Canada. This Canadian idea of the United Nations emergency force was a godsend. After a whole year of operation it has proved to be a great success and has provided security in Israel, so frequently heretofore endangered. The longer the United Nations police force stays in Aqaba and Gaza, the more established the role of this force becomes as an instrument to prevent hostilities. It might be a wise thing, therefore, to use an ounce of prevention by sending such an international peace force to other threatened borders.
It is, however, a sad fact to hear that the United Nations has difficulty in financing this expeditionary force, especially as a result of the Soviet bloc refusal to contribute to its upkeep. This is further proof of the Soviet union's lack of co-operation and lack of interest in preserving peace in troubled areas. In addition to using the United Nations police force on troubled borders, the United Nations' task of preserving peace in the Middle East will be well served if the Canadian delegation plays its part by encouraging the Arab states to recognize the fact that Israel is a real and permanent state in the Middle East and that a basis for co-existence should be found. By demanding the solving of the Arab refugee problem and by advocating a United Nations sponsored economic aid and technical development program our delegation will contribute a lot towards bringing stable conditions into the Middle East and the other countries in central Europe.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue my address in another official language which I admire and learned to speak while a student at Ottawa university.
(Translation):
And so, while the free world battles to check the rising tide of communism, it should not forget the victims of communism who sacrificed family possessions and even a career so as to be at the forefront of those who are fighting communist tyranny.
Have we so soon forgotten that we have celebrated the anniversaries of the revolt of the Polish workers at Poznan and of the Hungarian revolt in Budapest? We have been recently reminded of those anti-communist rebellions by the United Nations moral condemnation of Kremlin tyranny. We can all take pride in the fact that Canada, from the very beginning, played an

outstanding part in welcoming the refugees from communist oppression. According to Red Cross authorities, 30,000 refugees still remain in camps in Austria and Yugoslavia. To these must be added approximately 200,000 Poles, Slovaks, Lithuanians, Czechs and others who have fled various satellite countries. Those too have resisted communism and sacrificed all to recover their liberty. And yet on July 1st the Tory government all but slammed the door in their faces. Instead of applying a firm immigration policy it has acted in a fumbling and shameless way, making short work of one of its election promises. In his opening campaign speech in Toronto on April 25 last, the Prime Minister stated that the Conservatives would undertake an aggressive immigration policy, in co-operation with the provinces, in order to bring into Canada immigrants possessing the necessary skills and training. The Conservative government, he said, would increase and promote immigration, instead of hampering it. I feel that I should remind the present ministers that their duty now consists in taking immediate and fearless action in this regard.
Yesterday, during the ceremonies of Remembrance day, when paying tribute to our gallant soldiers, airmen and seamen, did we think of the supreme sacrifice they made during the first and second World Wars? Did we also recall the sacrifices of the French underground forces, of the heroes of the British 8th army in Italy, of the brave soldiers of the 3rd United States army in Prance, of the heroes of the R.A.F. and of the Polish squadrons during the battle of Britain? Did we forget about the sacrifice of the Polish artillery divisions at Mount-Cassino? Finally, last but not least, have we already forgotten the millions of human beings, Jews and Gentiles alike, who suffered and even died under dreadful tortures in Nazi concentration camps or in Russian forced labour camps? Let us not forget that what they died for is worth preserving now.
May I make further remarks in French, a language I so gladly learned to speak in the happy years when I was studying philosophy at the University of Ottawa. As a humble Torontonian, I was treated with courtesy and great kindness by the reverend Oblate Fathers and my French-Canadian fellow students. As a new member of the house, and on the occasion of my first speech here, let me publicly express to them my

appreciation and esteem. The various elements of French culture I have gathered there have been a welcome addition to my education.
In this 23rd parliament which looms so large in the history of Canadian politics, I am happy to find myself in the company of five colleagues from the medical profession. I am also particularly happy to find myself in the company of the first Canadians of Italian and Chinese descent to be members of the House of Commons. I daresay that I share their feelings unreservedly, being myself the first Canadian of Polish descent to sit in this honourable house.
I am also proud to represent the cosmopolitan constituency of Trinity which in the past elected such well-known members as Hugh Plaxton, Lionel Conacher, Donald Car-rick and Senator Roebuck. Like them, I wish to dedicate my life to the service of this, my native constituency. May I in this way show my gratitude towards Canada-"mon pays, mes amours", to use a phrase from the French Canadian song which I often sang on St. John the Baptist day.
Should I admit that I bend under the burden of so much dignity and responsibility imposed upon me by my duties as a representative of my fellow citizens? However, let me add at once that I take heart at the thought that, as the sole liberal member from the city of Toronto, I follow in the footsteps of a great parliamentarian and legal authority, the very distinguished former prime minister (Mr. St. Laurent), until recently leader of a Liberal government which gave our great country its most glowing years of harmony and economic development ever witnessed in our history. Bold and clear-minded architect of the full emancipation of our country, a statesman whom posterity will consider as a leading figure of the Liberal party, he saved world peace, on October 19, 1956, in directing the conduct of our representatives at the United Nations Organization. "Man's time being short," as mentioned in Holy Writ, this highly regarded leader wishes to leave the parliamentary scene. He will be remembered as one of the most important personalities in the political history of Canada. This man was a great leader and more particularly a great Canadian.
